the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing

if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.
  We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated
with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.

approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and

solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.
  We believe that our framework provides a flexible environment in which many
important problems can be studied leading to novel and important results.
Moreover, our approach provides a novel and general solution to the consistent
query answering problem which is important in practice.
  Finally, we point out some open problems, such as the following: (1) How to
define a semantics for functional dependencies involving transitivity? (2) How
to extend our framework in order to handle multivalued dependencies?

subject for database practitioners.

cheaper to do than building a new theoretical framework, it would demonstrate

  SiD is a detector design for the International Linear Collider (ILC) that was
validated in 2012. A final report was published in 2012 [1]. With a potential
construction date of the ILC moving closer, it is now the time to review the
design and technology decision that were made during the DBD phase and reconsider
them in the light of the recent technological advances. For each area of SiD
development this report will discuss the current design, the R&D needs and
opportunities for participation.
  The SiD collaboration is reactivating to address these R&D topics and
consider new technology developments that could impact the detector design.
Participation in this R&D is open to all interested parties. The SiD collaboration
welcomes this opportunity to work with industry and move forward detector
technology.

and discuss areas where R&D is needed or beneficial.

over-reliance on training labels and (2) limitation of object categories.

grow and learn new objects with unannotated 2D images. To achieve this goal,
we start from the observation that 2D images, from one species, can be
represented by an union-of-2D-Boxes (U2B) space, which is a hierarchical,
non-overlapping 2D box structure. Based on the U2B, we establish a
state-dependent mapping to represent the 2D-6D relationship of each 2D box in
a category-dependent manner with the concept of 2D-6D correlativity matrix
(D2C matrix). By initializing and updating the D2C matrices for each category,
our proposed framework, named as Matrix-Based 2D-6D (MB26D) framework, is able
to predict the 6D pose of objects that have similar 2D appearances to the
training images and can grow to new object categories that have similar 2D
annotations to the training images. The proposed MB26D framework is evaluated
on two public datasets, YCB-Video and LMO-1. The experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms two-stage pipelines and
direct methods, especially for objects with sufficient 2D training images.

global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized
$\theta$-terms. These introduce non-linear couplings between axion fields and
topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large
subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we
illustrate that we are in a regime where a large number of axion fields as
well as charged states are absent. As a consequence, the behavior of the
effective field theory is dominated by the presence of an infinite tower of
massless states, which leads to the conclusion that global symmetries are
absent.

connected to the presence of boundary magnetic sources for the axion fields in
a near-extremal, black-brane background. This leads to a related conjecture
which illustrates that generalized global symmetries are likely to be absent in
a large class of $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories that contain
axions.

could signal the breakdown of global symmetries and we discuss the connections
between the absence of global symmetries and the presence of generic
supersymmetry-breaking terms, such as the $\eta$-term.

  Chemical synthesis is a central aspect of many industries, including those
related to medicine, energy, and materials science. The field of machine
learning has shown considerable promise in facilitating this process by
predicting the properties of molecular structures and suggesting improvements.
While existing tools are quite effective, there are still situations where they
fall short. For instance, they often rely on approximate models that require
significant computational resources, or they focus on a specific property and
provide no alternatives when their predictions are wrong. In this paper, we
propose a framework that takes as input a molecular structure and outputs a
chemical compound with a desired property. It first predicts the property of
the input molecular structure using a fast and accurate model, and then
generates a "template" by carrying out a series of chemical reactions to its
neighboring molecules. The generated template is finally converted into a
chemical compound by predicting and satisfying the required structural and
chemical properties. We experimentally verify that the proposed framework can
be used to design chemical compounds with a variety of properties, and we
provide evidence of its usefulness by carrying out genetic optimization on a
real-world problem.

differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has

uses a unifying notation to outline some of the techniques used in the
transcription step of simultaneous direct methods (which
discretize-then-optimize) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization
problems. We focus on collocation, integrated residual and Runge-Kutta schemes.
These transcription methods are then applied to a simulation case study to
answer a question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, namely: If there are
not enough ventilators, is it possible to ventilate more than one patient on a
single ventilator? The results suggest that it is possible, in principle, to
estimate individual patient parameters sufficiently accurately, using a

disconnect a patient from the system or needing more than one flow rate sensor.

occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians

clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving

to what extent a computer can exploit additional knowledge from clinical

domain-knowledge based module which classifies each voxel based on the
corresponding domain knowledge. We show that the domain knowledge based module
can significantly improve the esophageal tumor segmentation on the NCANDatabase. Specifically, the domain knowledge based module has a superior performance
compared to traditional deep learning based approaches when validated on
images with additional knowledge available, while being inferior on images
without additional knowledge. This indicates that the additional knowledge can
indeed improve the segmentation performance, while also providing an
explanation of why a particular voxel was classified as part of the tumor.
This also shows that the additional knowledge can be exploited in a very
general computerizable way, without image modality specific assumptions.

about 10--125 times lower computational time compare to a common statistical
method, such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo. In addition, the
ensemble-based method can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Testing the method
on a case inspired from a real field also yielded accurate formation
evaluation. Thus, the proposed method has great potential to be applied in
real-time well logging interpretation.

extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract
information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in
which the named entities (NEs) can be nested since they often contain multiple
types. Although much progress has been made in Chinese nested NER in recent
years, it still faces a challenge of very long NEs. The conventional methods
handle the very long NEs by using character-level models which suffer from
data-hungry problem. To solve this problem, we propose a method called
Maximum Non-Overlapping Substrings (MOS) to deal with the very long NEs for
Chinese nested NER. The core idea is to represent each NE as a set of maximum
non-overlapping substrings and then use a linear model to classify the tuples
$(\text{NE}, \text{B-label}, \text{M-label}, \text{E-label})$. We evaluate our
method on two Chinese nested NER datasets. The experimental results indicate
that our method outperforms the character-level model by 3.38\% on average on
the coarse NER task while using much less training data.

  We consider the assessment of distribution systems after disruptions in
transportation and energy systems with private electric vehicles (EVs). To this
end, we propose a multi-agent optimization problem with equilibrium constraints
(MOPEC) to characterize the decentralized charging behavior of EV drivers and the
discrete operational decisions of distribution systems before and after
disruptions. However, solving the proposed model directly is computationally
challenging because of its non-convexity and high dimensionality. To address this
issue, we develop a decoupled scheme that contains convex programs to simultaneously
reformulate the decentralized problems of EV drivers and the discrete problem of
distribution systems. We further design an efficient computational algorithm
based on the reformulated convex programs to solve the reformulated problem of
EV drivers in parallel and then coupled with the reformulated problem of
distribution systems. Numerical studies are conducted to illustrate the
effectiveness of our modeling approach and the proposed computational method. The
results obtained reveal how private EVs can support the local energy needs
after disruptions and how the decentralized charging decisions of EVs affect the
potential islanding operation of distribution systems. We conclude that the
proposed modeling and computational approach can provide valuable insights for the
future assessment of transportation and energy systems with network

superior to that of a system using only discrete control.

their advantages and disadvantages with a view to suggesting areas of future
research.

the development of systems that can detect tumors in MRI images of patients with
different racial and ethnic backgrounds. This is a need driven by the fact that
such systems have been found to be racially and ethnically biased. The success
of such systems also depends on the development of techniques found in the area
of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These techniques include Deep Neural Networks

domain to be applied in other domains with minimal adaptation. The use of these
techniques has been found to yield excellent results but also raises some
theoretical issues especially with regards to the ownership of intellectual
property rights and the purpose for which such models are used.

extraction of features from MRI images which can be used in the diagnosis of

all these components as well as several image processing techniques that can be
used in their development.

efficient collection protocol for Wireless Sensor Networks. The former is the
Bidirectional Link Quality Estimation, which allows nodes to easily and quickly
compute the quality of a link between a pair of nodes. The latter, Hierarchical
Range Sectoring, organizes sensors in different sectors based on their location
within the network. Based on this organization, nodes from each sector are
coordinated to transmit in specific periods of time to reduce the hidden
terminal problem. To evaluate these two mechanisms, a protocol called HBCP
(Hierarchical-Based Collection Protocol), that implements both mechanisms, has
been implemented in TinyOS 2.1, and evaluated in a testbed using TelosB motes.
The results show that the HBCP protocol is able to achieve a very high
reliability, especially in large networks and in scenarios with bottlenecks.
Regarding the energy consumption, HBCP is efficient compared with traditional
protocols, as it tries to balance the number of transmissions with the
convergence of the network. A variation of HBCP, that turns off some sensors,
also showed to be efficient in networks with a large number of sensors.

  Entity recommendation is the task of recommending entities to users based on
their interaction history with a collection of entities. Wikipedia, as a
knowledge graph and community-built encyclopedia, contains hundreds of languages,
with a sizeable collection of entity categories and types, and a longitudinal
user interaction dataset in the form of page views. Despite its size and
interaction data, Wikipedia entity recommendation has received limited attention,
and the few existing approaches are ad-hoc and language-specific. One reason for
the lack of methods is the lack of a clear understanding of the data and its
properties. In this paper, we provide an extensive and systematic analysis of
Wikipedia as a knowledge graph and interaction data setting for entity
recommendation. We identify its benefits -- e.g., large scale and multi-language
settings -- and challenges -- e.g., sparse user interaction data and presence of
noise in the data.

transplantation (KT). The increasing shortage of kidney donors has driven the
development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but we are able to establish some structural
properties, and thus design efficient value function based algorithms to find
optimal policies. Numerical examples illustrate the significance of
incorporating the incompatibility factor into the proposed model by showing
significant suboptimality if the incompatibility is not taken into account.

procedures, and be used to compare different desensitization techniques.

ula choice for modeling dependence in
high dimensions. This broad class of copulas is introduced and surveyed,
including elliptical copulas, skew $t$ copulas, factor copulas, time series
copulas and regression copulas. The common auxiliary representation of implicit
copulas is outlined, and how this makes them both a dependent version of
univariate marginal models and a restricted version of general copula models.
Time series and factor copulas are then specialized further, as examples of
implicit copulas that are widely used in practice. Properties of implicit
copulas that make them useful are discussed, including parameterization ease,
model complexity and estimation convenience. Ways in which implicit copulas can
be extended or generalized are also considered, including mixtures, blends and
regenerated versions. Research avenues and new copula designs based on
time-series and factor copulas are proposed.
  We consider a factor copula model with independent factor copulas and discuss
how dependent factors lead to an increase in the estimation complexity. We
propose two methods for estimation: a simple moment estimation (ME) method and
a faster-than-expected alternating least squares (ALS) method. These estimation
methods are compared against the established likelihood-based estimation (LBE)
method, which is known to be computationally expensive due to its need for
Monte Carlo simulation. We lead with an example study on stock returns from 11
countries, showing that all three estimation methods lead to similar factor
copula models in terms of copula parameter values and dependence structures.
However, the new simpler ME and ALS estimation methods significantly reduce
estimation time, by factors of 25 and 5, respectively. We conclude that both
the ME and ALS methods are viable alternatives to LBE for factor copula data.
Ten open data sets are also provided for further research.
  Factor copulas are introduced as dependent copulas that can capture several
types of factors at the same time. A moment estimation algorithm is provided
for easily estimating the parameters of several factor copulas at the same time
without the need for Monte Carlo simulation. Several factor copula models are
constructed and analyzed using stock returns from around the world. The
dependent structures introduced by the factor copulas are found to be meaningful
and to lead to an improvement in portfolio returns. Two novel factor copula
designs are also introduced, one that adds time variation to a factor copula and
another that adds a latent variable to a factor copula.

model, especially when it is equipped with the Skip-gram learning scheme. Our
goal is to explain how embeddings, that are now widely used in NLP (Natural
Language Processing), are influenced by the distribution of terms in the
documents of the considered corpus. We use a mathematical formulation to shed
light on how the decision to use such a model makes implicit assumptions on the
structure of the language. We show how Markovian assumptions, that we discuss,
lead to a very clear theoretical understanding of the formation of embeddings,
and in particular the way it captures what we call frequentist synonyms. These
assumptions allow to produce generative models and to conduct an explicit
analysis of the loss function commonly used by these NLP techniques. Moreover,
we produce synthetic corpora with different levels of structure and show
empirically how the word2vec algorithm succeed, or not, to learn them. It leads
us to empirically assess the capability of such models to capture structures on
a corpus of around 42 millions of financial News covering 12 years. That for,
we rely on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists largely used on financial
texts and we show that embeddings are exposed to mixing terms with opposite
polarity, because of the way they can treat antonyms as frequentist synonyms.
Beside we study the non-stationarity of such a corpus and the evolution of
language, by computing non-stationary distributions over time. Again, our
analysis on small corpora and experiments lead us to claim that all the
statistical analysis should be performed at the level of a year, and that it
leads to a loss of non-stationarity, that is the main contribution of this
work.

linguistics rely on unary modalities to allow for the controlled application of
structural rules affecting word order and phrase structure. These controlled
structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by
the original Lambek Calculus or its pregroup simplification. Proposals for
compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  From a category theoretic perspective, we provide a new formulation of the
Frobenius-algebra model of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps. Our formulation avoids the need for
twisting of morphisms by using instead additional morphisms in a monoidal
category. This approach provides a semantically motivated view of the
"twisting" as a way of combining interpretations in a monoidal category. As
an application of our formulation, we show how the proposal can be extended to
handle multiple ambiguity types simultaneously.
  Our method provides a way of representing co-existing interpretations of
ambiguous utterances and provides a uniform framework for the integration of
lexical and derivational ambiguity. As a practical application, we show how our
approach can be used to study the ambiguity of German word order and provide an
interpretation of basic sentences in the vector space of spin states. Our
theoretical framework provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for the
connection between type-logical grammar and formal quantum mechanics.
  In this paper we extend the density matrix semantics of the vectorial
interpretation of the extended Lambek Calculus to `yes-no' questions. We show
how the interpretation of basic sentences is extended to cover sentences
involving multiple alternative hypotheses. As an application of our formulation
we study the ambiguity of German multiple-choice questions and provide an
interpretation in the space of density matrices.

finding equilibria is to learn
rationalizable behavior, where players learn to avoid iteratively dominated
actions. However, even in the basic setting of multiplayer general-sum games,
existing algorithms require a number of samples exponential in the number of
players to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper
develops the first line of efficient algorithms for learning rationalizable
Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) whose sample
complexities are polynomial in all problem parameters including the number of
players. To achieve this result, we also develop a new efficient algorithm for
the simpler task of finding one rationalizable action profile (not necessarily
an equilibrium), whose sample complexity substantially improves over the best
existing results of Wu et al. (2021). Our algorithms incorporate several novel
techniques to guarantee rationalizability and no (swap-)regret simultaneously,
including a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which
may be of independent interest. We complement our results with a sample
complexity lower bound showing the sharpness of our guarantees.
  We also extend our analysis to study the problem of learning rationalizable
CE that are "simple" in the sense of having few mixed strategies. This line of
work is motivated by the observation that most existing algorithms produce
CE that have an exponential number of mixed strategies, which may not be
desirable in practice. Our main result is that, for the setting of large
action spaces, even the simplest of algorithms (such as Freq-Play) can produce
CE with few mixed strategies provided the number of players is large enough.
This result shows a interesting tradeoff between the number of players and
the number of mixed strategies in defining "simple" rationalizable CE. For the
setting of small action spaces, we show a negative result: there exists a gap
between the sample complexity of all existing algorithms and the lower bound we
prove in the general setting.
  Finally, we discuss how our results can be used to improve the sample
complexity of several problems that are relevant in multiagent learning, such
as learning separable games and learning games with oblivious actions.

allows agents to remember by reusing historical observations. However, the
uniform reuse strategy that treats all observations equally overlooks the

exact ergodic capacity (EC) of a
point-to-point multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system assisted by an
intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). In addition, we account for the effects
of correlated Rayleigh fading and the intertwinement between the amplitude and
the phase shift of the reflecting coefficient of each IRS element, which are
usually both neglected despite their presence in practice. Random matrix theory
tools allow to derive the probability density function (PDF) of the EC in a
closed-form expression, which depends on the statistics of the channel and the
phase shifts. Then, to facilitate practical deployment, we maximize the EC with
respect to the phase shifts with low overhead. Specifically, we exploit an
asymptotic analysis to find the jointly optimal phase shifts that maximize the
EC in the high-IRS- dimension and available power per dimension limits. We also
derive a convenient convergence criterion that indicates when we can switch to
the asymptotic analysis. In addition, we derive a suboptimal per-element based
scheme, which has a lower computational overhead, and is also capable of
tapping significant capacity gains. Simulation results verify the correctness
of our theoretical analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed
strategies.

departure from Newtonian dynamics beyond a radius of $\approx 10$ kAU, partly
because I use $2\sigma$ outlier rejection to clean their sample first.
Nonetheless, the uncertainties are small enough that existing WB data are
nearly sufficient to distinguish Newtonian dynamics from Modified Newtonian
Dynamics. I estimate that $\approx 1000$ WB systems will be required for this
purpose if using only line velocities.

systematics like undetected companions and contamination by dynamical binaries
or stellar clusters.

measured, it will be difficult to distinguish between different theories of
gravity on the outskirts of the galaxy.

"combined method"). While this does help to constrain the velocity dispersion,
the improvement is not large enough to be of great use for distinguishing
different theories of gravity.

than measuring the dispersion directly from proper motions (which are generally
more precise than line velocities).

constrain the density profile of the galaxy in a way that is independent of the

learning from a sequence of few-shot learning tasks on an imbalanced dataset.

classify streams of visual information from an imbalanced few-shot learning
dataset. At each learning step, InconSP learns from a few categories on the new
data while trying to forget the previously learned ones in order to minimize the
overall error throughout the learning process. InconSP is able to tackle both
the incremental and few-shot learning aspects of the problem and does not require

incremental few-shot learning models that only learn from new categories at
evaluation time. We also show that InconSP performs better than non-incremental
few-shot learning models on a sequence of learning tasks.

determination of the CKM angle $\gamma$ from
tree--level decays is presented. Up to 16 independent determinations, using a
variety of beauty and charm mesons decay modes, are available at LHCb. Not all
of them have the same sensitivity to $\gamma$. The best accuracy is reached by
combining all of the available results. These proceedings review some of the
independent determinations used in the combination and present the latest
combined result available, as of Summer 2018.

results from two-body decays $B^+ \to D^+ D^+ X$ and $B^+ \to D^0 (D^0
\overline{D^0}) X$, is presented. The latest combined result is $\gamma =
(67.8 \pm 2.0)^\circ$, with an uncertainty reduced by a factor of three with
respect to the previous latest combination. The uncertainty is expected to
decrease even further with more data.
  New independent determinations not included in the latest combination are
also presented. In particular, two new two-body decay modes $B^0_{s} \to
K^+ \overline{K^0} $ and $B^0_{s} \to K^0 \overline{K^+} $ have entered the
world average with a relatively large weight. A interesting feature of these
modes is that they have a similar sensitivity to $\gamma$ than the modes in the
current latest combination.
  Finally, prospects for improving the accuracy of the angle $\gamma$ at LHCb
are discussed. With the full LHC Run 2 data sample and the upgrade of the
detector, LHCb will be able to perform new measurements in decay modes which
were not accessible before. In addition, a new experiment, the Long-Lived
Beauty Meson experiment (LLBM) at the Future Circular Collider (FCC), is
expected to measure $\gamma$ with an uncertainty better than one degree.

surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is mainly based on ventricular volume and function according to current
guidelines. Both of these two biomarkers are most reliably assessed by
segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. In several grand
challenges in the last years, U-Net architectures have shown impressive results
on the provided data. However, in clinical practice, data sets are more diverse
considering individual pathologies and image properties derived from different
scanner properties. Additionally, specific training data for complex rare
diseases like TOF is scarce.
  For this work, 1) we assessed the accuracy gap when using a publicly
available labelled data set (the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC)
data set) for training and subsequent applying it to CMR data of TOF patients
and vice versa and 2) whether we can achieve similar results when applying the
model to a more heterogeneous data base.
  Multiple deep learning models were trained with four-fold cross validation.
Afterwards they were evaluated on the respective unseen CMR images from the
other collection. Our results confirm that current deep learning models can
achieve excellent results (left ventricle dice of
$0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ train/validation) however a significant
accuracy drop can be observed when applying the models on CMR data of TOF
patients when being trained on the ACDC data set (dice $0.813\pm{0.014}$/
$0.796\pm{0.016}$ train/validation). Vice versa even better results than
reported in the literature were achieved.
  The results indicate that current deep learning models require large and
diverse labelled data sets when being applied to rare diseases like TOF or
possibly other complex heart diseases.
  Furthermore, this work underlines once more the importance of CMR image
quality. Simple filters could be applied to increase the accuracy on the ACDC
data set.
  In summary, our work highlights the need for large and diverse data bases
and possibly new approaches when training and evaluating deep learning models
for CMR image segmentation in patients with congenital heart disease.

backbone to look at all objects in the FPN-based detection frameworks.
Specifically, one is to introduce auxiliary objective functions to make each
backbone level directly receive the back-propagation signals from all objects
via FPN. The other is to introduce the feature reuse to enable each backbone
backpropagation path to cover more objects. Extensive experiments on the
COCO benchmark validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, which
shows that the detection performance of large-scale objects can be significantly
improved by introducing FPN. Moreover, our method is simple, efficient, and

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). In
language, words of the same form can take different meanings depending on
context. While humans easily infer the meaning or gloss of such words by their
context, machines stumble on this task.As such, we intend to replicated and
expand upon the results of Huang et al.GlossBERT, a model which they design to
disambiguate these words (Huang et al.,2019). Specifically, we propose the
following augmentations: data-set tweaking(alpha hyper-parameter), ensemble
methods, and replacement of BERT with BART andALBERT. The following GitHub
repository contains all code used in this report, which extends on the code
made available by Huang et al.
  We obtain hyper-parameter sensitive results that are competitive with the
current state-of-the-art. Ensembling also yields an increase in accuracy.
Finally, we observe that while BART does not perform better than GlossBERT, it
does at least maintain its accuracy while being 1.5GB smaller.
  Future work could also look at looking at other data-preprocessing
techniques such as over-sampling, undersampling, and scaling. One could also
look at other state-of-the-art models such as T5 and BLOOM on this task.
Besides that, there are many other NLP tasks that one could try to tackle as
well.

and reason about real world task procedures, which often requires thorough
understanding of temporal common sense and multimodal information, as these
procedures are often communicated through a combination of texts and images.
Such capability is essential for applications such as sequential task planning
and multi-source instruction summarization. While humans are capable of
reasoning about and sequencing unordered multimodal procedural instructions,
whether current machine learning models have such essential capability is still
an open question. In this work, we benchmark models' capability of reasoning
over and sequencing unordered multimodal instructions by curating datasets from
popular online instructional manuals and collecting comprehensive human
annotations. We find models not only perform significantly worse than humans
but also seem incapable of efficiently utilizing the multimodal information. To
improve machines' performance on multimodal event sequencing, we propose
sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that exploit the sequential
alignment properties of both texts and images, resulting in > 5% significant
improvements.
  Our study reveals machines' limited capability of reasoning over and sequencing
unordered multimodal instructions and provides practical solutions to improve
such capability, which has the potential to benefit a wide range of applications
that rely on understanding and reasoning about real world task procedures.

multiple-output (XL-MIMO)
systems are seen as a promising technology for providing very high data rates
in increased user-density scenarios. Spatial non-stationarities and visibility
regions (VRs) appear across the XL-MIMO array since its large dimension is of
the same order as the distances to the user-equipments (UEs). Due to the
increased density of UEs in typical applications of XL-MIMO systems and the
scarcity of pilots, the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling
algorithms become challenging. In this paper, we propose a joint RA and
scheduling protocol, namely non-overlapping VR XL- MIMO (NOVR-XL) RA protocol,
which takes advantage of the different VRs of the UEs for improving RA
performance. First, we model the VRs around the UEs as ellipses located at
their positions and oriented along the up/down directions. Then, we define the
non-overlapping condition among the VRs and gather UEs in exclusive groups
according to this condition. The UEs in each group are those with non-overlapping
VRs and are called group-UEs. We propose a fast RA scheme for the group-UEs
operating in different subarrays of the XL-MIMO array, located at the center of
the non-overlapping VRs, whereas the remaining UEs, called ungroup-UEs, employ
a conventional RA scheme. We present a joint scheduling framework in which
optimization problems are formulated to solve for the assignment of UEs to
subarrays, as well as for the detection sequence and the data rate allocation.
The proposed NOVR-XL RA protocol is able to increase the number of successful
RA attempts compared to conventional RA schemes, while keeping the overhead
frame length small. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme achieves
significant gains in terms of successful RA attempts, spectrum efficiency, and
connection throughput, as compared to conventional RA schemes.

this gate design through numerical simulations on chains of two to 33 ions.

attractive choice for decoupling in the presence of motional heating, where the
laser frequency may not be well stabilized.

Molmer-Sorensen gate arises from the large differential laser phase that can
develop between the cooling lasers and the modulation laser, which can pull
the motional mode out of the Sisyphus decoupling, causing oscillations in the
fidelity. This complication can be avoided by using optical elements that the
cooling and modulation lasers can pass through equally, such as parabolic
reflectors or a photonic crystal fiber.

robust gates such as the Szydagov gate to produce a comprehensive set of
frequency robust gates for ion surgery and wavefront engineering.

Sagnac interferometer which is normally used to calibrate the angular momentum
of a gyroscope. The spectral shift in the rotating gyroscope is explained with
respect to the longitudinal Doppler shift of the counter propagating beams in
the Sagnac interferometer.
  From the theoretical calculation it is found that there is a spectral shift
only around the rest frequency of the gyroscope and also the amount of spectral
shift depends on the rotation rate of the gyroscope. The predicted values of
the spectral shift are found good agreement with the experimental results.
Therefore, the proposed explanation of spectral shift in the rotating
gyroscope may be useful for advanced gyroscope.
  In view of applications of the gyroscope, it may be useful to explain the
gyroscopic effect in a single photon.
  Finally, it is found that the proposed explanation of spectral shift may be
applicable for all types of gyroscope.
  Thus, the reported observation and proposed explanation may be an excellent
pedagogical example to understand both the gyroscope and Sagnac interferometer
for the advanced students.

Sections for Parabolic adjoint action in type $A$]. Let $G$ be an irreducible
simple algebraic group and $B$ a Borel subgroup of $G$. Let $\mathfrak n$ be
the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $B$. Consider an irreducible subgroup $P$
of $G$ containing $B$. Let $P'$ be the derived group of $P$. Let $\mathfrak m$
be the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $P$. A theorem of Richardson asserts
that the algebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$ of $P$ semi-invariants is
multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety $e+V$ such that the restriction map
induces an isomorphism of $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$ onto $\mathbb C[e+V]$
is called a Weierstrass section for the action of $P'$ on $\mathfrak m$. Here
in type $A$ such a section is constructed, but in better form than that given
in Sect. 4, loc cit. Yet the main difference is a complete change of emphasis
from the construction of a Weierstrass section, to its application.
  Let $\mathscr N(P)$ be the set of nilpotent elements in $\mathfrak m$ under
the action of $P'$. It is a variety. A typical problem is to describe
component-wise a subvariety $X_\tau$ of $\mathscr N(P)$ such that
$\mathscr N(P)(\mathbb R)$ intersects $X_\tau(\mathbb R)$ in a finite set of
points. A tool to that effect is to describe the characteristic polynomial of
the trace map associated to the action of $P'$ on $\mathscr N(P)$. It is an
example of a polynomial studied by Lusztig in a different context. The
notation introduced here for a Schur polynomial $P_{r|n}$ is particularly
adapted for $r=n$. It is used repeatedly in the process of induction from
$3$ to $n$ starting from the description of $X_3$. The final result,
$X_n$, is also interesting in its own right and its description does not
require the induction process.

  Language models (LM) are pre-trained models that can predict the
probability distribution of the next word in a given sequence of words in a
language. LM is a fundamental tool in natural language processing (NLP) and
has been widely used as a component in many generation applications, such as
text summarization and machine translation. Recently, pre-trained models like
BART and T5 have achieved promising results in generating text in various
languages. However, we find that the generated text does not always match the
language, culture and grammar of the target language, indicating that the
language model may not be tailored to the specific language. In this paper, we
propose to transfer a language model from one language to a similar language
by fine-tuning the model on the target language. We experiment with transferring
a BART model from English to five other languages (i.e., German, Spanish, French,
Italian, and Portuguese). Our results show that the transfer achieves
significant improvements over BART models that are only trained on general
data in English. We also find that the transfer achieves better performance
than models that are trained from scratch in the target language. We release
our code at https://github.com/ghru

iOCR. iOCR was developed with a spell correction algorithm to fix errors
introduced by conventional OCR for vote tabulation. The results found that the
iOCR system outperforms conventional OCR techniques.
  From the user perspective, iOCR provides a list of possible corrections for
each scanned ballot. The user can then select the correct output. The scan
quality and the size of the image do not affect the performance of iOCR. From
the technical perspective, iOCR produces high-quality text that can be
accurately compared with the mark-based ballots. The character error rate of
iOCR is less than 2%.
  In conclusion, iOCR is a reliable postprocessing technique for scans of
paper ballots. It can improve the accuracy of conventional OCR techniques and
provide a satisfactory solution for electoral authorities who use digital
ballots.

pathogens from being leaked from the facility. An NPR maintains a negative
pressure inside with respect to the outside reference space so that microbes
are contained inside of an NPR. Nowadays, differential pressure sensors (DPSs)
are utilized by the Building Management Systems (BMSs) to control and monitor
the negative pressure in an NPR. This paper demonstrates a non-invasive and
stealthy attack on NPRs by spoofing a DPS at its resonant frequency. Our
contributions are: (1) We show that DPSs used in NPRs typically have resonant
frequencies in the audible range. (2) We use this finding to design malicious
music to create resonance in DPSs, resulting in an overshooting in the DPS's
normal pressure readings. (3) We show how the resonance in DPSs can fool the
BMSs so that the NPR turns its negative pressure to a positive one, causing a
potential \textit{leak} of deadly microbes from NPRs. We do experiments on 8
DPSs from 5 different manufacturers to evaluate their resonant frequencies
considering the sampling tube length and find resonance in 6 DPSs. We can
achieve a 2.5 Pa change in negative pressure from a resonant DPS, which is the
same as a BSL-4's required negative pressure. This change is sufficient to
make a NPR to leak microbes. We also show that our scheme can be used to
create a persistent high pressure in DPSs, which can also cause a leak from
an NPR. Our attack cost is $35 and lasts for 5 minutes, considering a normal
operation of an NPR between 10 minutes to 30 minutes. Our attack can cause
serious harms as it can spread deadly microbes from an NPR. Therefore, we
recommend that DPSs in life-critical applications should be tested for their
resonant frequencies during the design and deployment phases.

test for DPSs, especially in life-critical biolabs and hospitals.

a design requirement for the sensors meant to be used in NPRs and other
life-critical applications.

of firming in low-carbon grids. A
common concern raised from ex-post assessments is that storage resources can
fail to respond to strong price signals during times of scarcity. While
commonly attributed to forecast error or failures in operations, we posit that
this behavior can be explained from the perspective of risk-averse scheduling.
Using a stochastic self-scheduling framework and real-world data harvested from
the Australian National Electricity Market, we demonstrate that risk-averse
storage resources tend to have a myopic operational perspective, that is, they
typically engage in near-term price arbitrage and chase only few extreme price
spikes and troughs, thus remaining idle in several time periods with markedly
high and low prices. This has important policy implications for storage market
design in Australian-style markets and, more broadly, any market considering
storage self-scheduling.

simplified (linear) boundary layer friction, a Newtonian cooling scheme and dry
convective adjustment. A series of controlled experiments are conducted by
varying planetary rotation rate and imposed equator-to-pole temperature
difference. These defining parameters are cast into dimensionless forms to
establish a parameter space, in which different circulation regimes are mapped
and classified. Clear trends are found when varying planetary rotation rate and
frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The sequence of circulation
regimes as a function of planetary rotation rate strongly resembles that
obtained in laboratory experiments on rotating, stratified flows, especially if
a topographic $\beta$-effect is included in those experiments to emulate the
planetary vorticity gradients induced by the spherical curvature of the planet.
A regular baroclinic wave regime is also obtained at intermediate values of
thermal Rossby number and its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber
depend strongly on the strength of radiative and frictional damping. These
regular waves exhibit some strong similarities to baroclinic storms observed on
Mars under some conditions. Multiple jets are found at the highest rotation
rates, when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related length scales
are much smaller than the radius of the planet. These multi-jet circulation
regimes are qualitatively similar to 3D global MHD simulations of planetary
electrodynamics at sub-stellar rotation rates.

studies of planetary climate by clearly demonstrating the regime diagram for a
 circulation system that can be expected to be present on slowly to moderately
rotating planets with significant global-scale horizontal temperature
gradients. It emphasizes the importance of considering the circulation regime
as a free variable in exoplanetary characterization and searches for life.

can be directly scaled to a specific planet, it demonstrates how different
circulation regimes are connected by controlled variations of two fundamental
dimensionless parameters. It provides a basis for further investigations of
state-of-the-art GCMs and helps to guide their interpretation by providing a
theoretical framework that shows how different circulation regimes are expected
to be connected by controlled variations of two fundamental dimensionless

agent filters the anomalous instances based on a human rule-based procedure
(which is considered safe), gets the human labels, applies geometric data

datasets. We get an improvement in accuracy and trust score with just few
additional labels compared to a baseline approach.
  Which instances to label is a challenging problem, especially in large-scale
situations. Typically, humans label the instances that are farthest from the
model's distribution, but that requires expertise and trust in the model. To
make the interaction more effective, we propose to use both trust and distance
as their priorities. To do this, we model the problem as a multi-objective
optimization one and use NSGA-II as our solver. We evaluate the parser agent
on MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets. We get an improvement in accuracy and trust
score with significantly fewer human labels compared to the baseline approach.
As a result, the cost of labeling decreases, and the benefit in accuracy and
trust increases.

of differential privacy (DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated us to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective. In this
work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss challenges
and promising applications, including the GNN domain. We compare and separate
works into graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs. Finally, we
conclude with a discussion of open questions and potential directions for further
research in this area.

discussed in the following sections. Here, we focus on the underlying
formulations of DP and privacy metrics, which are crucial for guaranteeing
privacy in graph settings.

systems. In this work we derive, within the positive-P phase-space formalism, a
new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose
gases. It goes beyond existing hydrodynamic approaches, such as superfluid
hydrodynamics or generalized hydrodynamics, in its capacity to simulate the
full quantum dynamics of these systems: it possesses the ability to compute
non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena.
Using this description, we derive a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme
which is able to simulate such non-equilibrium situations for longer times than
the full positive-P approach, at the expense of approximating the treatment of
quantum fluctuations, and show that this linearized scheme can be directly
connected with existing Bogoliubov approaches. Furthermore, we go on to
demonstrate the usefulness and advantages of this formalism by exploring the
correlations that arise in a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its
predictions to other established quantum many-body approaches.

function, the other being proportional to the specific relative entropy of the
observed law of letters w.r.t.\ the reference law of letters, obtained by
concatenating the words and randomising the location of the origin. The
proportionality constant equals the tail exponent of the renewal process.
  The purpose of the present paper is to extend both LDP's to letter sequences
that are not i.i.d. It is shown that both LDP's carry over when the letter
sequence satisfies a mixing condition called \emph{summable variation}. The
rate functions are again given by specific relative entropies w.r.t.\ the
reference law of words (annealed) or words plus letters (quenched).

which makes it a popular object of study in the theory of stochastic processes.

reflective elements capable of tuning the phase, amplitude, and frequency of the
impedance to optimize the wireless channel. The joint optimization of the IRS
and the active transceiver architecture is expected to bring significant
performance gains, but the associated problem formulations will be challenging
and computationally expensive due to the large number of degrees of freedom
associated with the IRS. In this paper, we propose a novel transceiver-IRS
design framework that enables the decoupling of the optimization from the
resolution of an over-determined linear system. Specifically, we show that a
smaller size of the active transceiver together with a specific dimension of
the reflective elements of the IRS, enables the formation of a low-rank plus
diagonal (LPD) matrix model of the combined transceiver-IRS channel. Then, we
propose a novel joint optimization framework, called LFD-Opt, which is capable
of exploiting the LPD structure to facilitate efficient joint transceiver-IRS
design. The LFD-Opt problem is non-convex and mixed-type, which impedes the

variables. We validate the proposed LFD-Opt framework through extensive
simulation experiments, showing that it offers considerable performance gains
over several baselines, for 5G and 6G wireless systems.

number of continual learning methods based on pretrained models have been
proposed. Some of these methods design continual learning mechanisms on the
pre-trained representations and only allow minimum updates or even no updates
of the backbone models during the training of continual learning. In this
paper, we question whether the complexity of these models is needed to achieve
good performance by comparing them to a simple baseline that we designed. We
argue that the pretrained feature extractor itself can be strong enough to
achieve a competitive or even better continual learning performance on
Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To validate this, we conduct a very
simple baseline that 1) use the frozen pretrained model to extract image
features for every class encountered during the continual learning stage and
compute their corresponding mean features on training data, and 2) predict the
class of the input based on the nearest neighbor distance between test samples
and mean features of the classes; i.e., Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This
baseline is single-headed, exemplar-free, and can be task-free (by updating the
means continually). This baseline achieved 88.53% on 10-Split-CIFAR-100,
surpassing most state-of-the-art continual learning methods that are all
initialized using the same pretrained transformer model. We hope our baseline
may encourage future progress in designing learning systems that can make full
use of the power of pretrained models.

data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
due to data reshuffling. Here we investigate this additional source of
variability, asking how depends on the number of folds and data dimensions.

an understudied area. Here we investigate how public sector officials
self-assess their dependency on the Google Web search engine, whether they are
aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to
retrieve all relevant information, and how much relevant information may
actually be missed due to Web search personalisation. We find that the majority
of participants in our experimental study are neither aware that there is a
potential problem nor do they have a strategy to mitigate the risk of missing
relevant information when performing online searches. Most significantly, we
provide empirical evidence that up to 20% of relevant information may be missed
due to Web search personalisation. This work has significant implications for
Web research by public sector professionals, who should be provided with
training about the potential algorithmic biases that may affect their judgments
and decision making, as well as clear guidelines how to minimise the risk of
missing relevant information.

design parameters for several collider configurations, and illustrate the

map toward development are also given.

perspectives. This report summarizes the main findings of the study group.

potential science, technical feasibility and cost estimates. The study group
concludes that a Muon Collider with an energy range of 1 to 30 TeV is

provide a quality metric specific to RDF data. To tackle these issues, QuadQA
provides a quality metric for RDF triples considering invalid triples and
provides a highly scalable framework to analyze large Linked Data datasets.

minutes. QuadQA has been used to analyze over 100,000,000,000 quads available
online over the internet.

details of each quality metric used by QuadQA. QuadQA has been used to analyze

scalable.

and contains over 4.7 billion quads. DBpedia is used by over thousands of

knowledge graph. For example, a web developer can use this metric to decide
which part of the knowledge graph to use in her application. A researcher can

metrics provided by QuadQA.

the description of `what-if' scenarios that integrate complex sequences of
workloads and faultloads.
  Frisbee offers a declarative domain-specific language (DDL) allowing users to
define the configuration of the testbed, the behavior of the application under
test (AUT), and the testing scenario which ties these two components together.
The DDL is parsed into a executable plan, which is executed by a controller in
charge of driving the testbed towards the desired behavior. This plan contains
sequences of workload/faultload transactions, which are implemented as containerized
commands that interact with the AUT via its APIs. Frisbee defines a modular
design where testing strategies, validation techniques, and testbed configurations
are decoupled, allowing easy extension and customization by the end-user.
Furthermore, Frisbee is designed with extensibility in mind, making it feasible
for adding support for new platforms, languages, and testing methodologies.
Testing strategies can be extended by adding custom validation routines,
configuring or extending the framework's testing strategies, or defining
completely new strategies by leveraging the framework's modular design. The
testing strategies are decoupled from the rest of the framework allowing for
easy customization and extension by the end-user. For example, stress testing
is configured by defining a stress testing strategy in a configuration file,
while a performance testing strategy might require the use of specialized
tools, such as Apache JMeter.

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.

model that can be used to synthesize HD maps with actor insertions and attributes
from sensor readings of the surrounding environment; (2) We propose a
novel actor insertion module that enables SceneGen to model actor density
marginals; (3) We present two perception benchmarks experiments that show
SceneGen can be used to improve the robustness of perception models.

related work; sections 3 and 4 detail the two key components of SceneGen;
sections 5 and 6 demonstrate how SceneGen can be used to train perception
models; section 7 shows how SceneGen can be extended to HD maps; and section 8
concludes this work.

the development and analysis of such structure-preserving discretisation

properties and proposals for novel schemes that achieve both high-order
accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the continuum

major downside to these schemes is that their structure-preserving properties
generally rely on exact solution of the (possibly nonlinear) systems of
equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. For small to moderate
systems, this is often feasible using current computing technology. However, as
the size of the systems increases (as it must if detailed it is to capture the
dynamics of interest in the continuum problem) solving them becomes increasingly
impractical. This is particularly the case for problems defined on very fine
spatial grids. In this paper, we propose a multigrid scheme for solving the
linear systems arising from the time-stepping step of a structure-preserving
scheme for a class of time-dependent PDEs. The scheme we propose retains all of
the local structure-preserving properties of the full-space scheme (e.g. it
retains exactly the conservation law(s) of the continuum equation) and has a
computational cost of only a small constant factor times that of the baseline
multigrid solver. To construct the scheme we show how to define a coarse-grid
version of the full-space scheme's spatial discretisation that retains all of
its local structure-preserving properties. This is then combined with a

from start to finish. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our scheme by
computing solutions to several examples, including one example in which the

cluster gravitational potential and self-gravity of the parent cloud. It also
considers radiative cooling (including that induced by dust) and a
state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. As shown
before, a superbubble embedded into a clumpy medium becomes highly distorted,

results indicate that in the case of massive ($\sim10^7$M$_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds, hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$), grain

yr$^{-1}$. In this manner, the produced (by sequential SNe) small dust grains
remain stable for a longer period (of the order of $10^8$ years), increasing
their likelihood of incorporation into giant molecular clouds. We conclude that
the interaction with clumps is a more efficient dust enrichment mechanism than
the supershell in the low metallicity superbubbles.

certain distance from an observer, e.g., $>$50m. Far3Det is particularly
important for autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating at highway speeds, which
require detections of far-field obstacles to ensure sufficient braking
distances. However, contemporary AV benchmarks such as nuScenes underemphasize
this problem because they evaluate performance only up to a certain distance
(50m). One reason is that obtaining far-field 3D annotations is difficult,
particularly for lidar sensors that produce very few point returns for far-away
objects. Indeed, we find that almost 50% of far-field objects (beyond 50m)
contain zero lidar points. Secondly, current metrics for 3D detection employ a
"one-size-fits-all" philosophy, using the same tolerance thresholds for near
and far objects, inconsistent with tolerances for both human vision and stereo
disparities. Both factors lead to an incomplete analysis of the Far3Det task.
For example, while conventional wisdom tells us that high-resolution RGB
sensors should be vital for 3D detection of far-away objects, lidar-based
methods still rank higher compared to RGB counterparts on the current benchmark
leaderboards. As a first step towards a Far3Det benchmark, we develop a method
to find well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset that contain many
objects beyond 50m. Our analysis shows that simply filtering out these far-away
objects improves the performance of 3D detection models significantly. We then
develop a simple protocol for evaluating Far3Det metrics that distinguish
itself from the current setting by using tolerance thresholds that vary with
distance. Our analysis shows that current 3D detection models have a significant
gap to the proposed Far3Det metrics, and future research is needed to close the
gap.

on laparoscopic liver surgery, where we register the organ model obtained from
a preoperative CT scan to the intraoperative partial organ surface,
reconstructed from the laparoscopic video. This is a challenging task due to
sparse and noisy intraoperative data, real-time requirements and many unknowns
- such as tissue properties and boundary conditions. Furthermore, establishing
correspondences between pre- and intraoperative data can be extremely difficult
since the liver usually lacks distinct surface features and the used imaging
modalities suffer from very different types of noise. In this work, we train a
convolutional neural network to perform both the search for surface
correspondences as well as the non-rigid registration in one step. The network
is trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly
generated, deforming organ-like structures. This enables the network to
immediately generalize to a new patient organ without the need to re-train. We
add various amounts of noise to the intraoperative surfaces during training,
making the network robust to noisy intraoperative data. During inference, the
network outputs the displacement field which matches the preoperative volume to
the partial intraoperative surface. In multiple experiments, we show that the
network translates well to real data while maintaining a high inference speed.
Our code is made available online.

state-of-the-art registration techniques. By evaluating the registration
accuracy as well as the computation time, we show that our method achieves
state-of-the-art accuracy while being significantly faster than the compared
methods. Additionally, we evaluate the robustness of our method with respect to
several factors including varying tissue properties, different boundary
conditions as well as different amounts of noise.

of a dynamic 3D scene. Motion vectors have shown to be beneficial for
downstream tasks such as action classification and collision avoidance.
However, data collected via LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras are computation
and labor intensive to precisely annotate for scene flow. We address this
annotation bottleneck on two ends. We propose a 3D scene flow benchmark and a
novel self-supervised setup for training flow models. The benchmark consists of
datasets designed to study individual aspects of flow estimation in progressive
order of complexity, from a single object in motion to real-world scenes.

estimation. The flow model is fed with sequences of point clouds to perform
flow estimation. A second model learns a latent metric to distinguish between
the points translated by the flow estimations and the target point cloud. This
latent metric is learned via a Multi-Scale Triplet loss, which uses
intermediary feature vectors for the loss calculation. We use our proposed
benchmark to draw insights about the performance of the baselines and of
different models when trained using our setup. We find that our setup is able
to keep motion coherence and preserve local geometries, which many
self-supervised baselines fail to grasp. Dealing with occlusions, on the other

a novel technique for automatically
learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, we show that hardening the system with Timeloops reduces the
success rate of EVA-based attacks from 81% to 0% for some microservices
applications and reduces the success rate from 100% to 82% for other microservices
applications.

competing for space in regular lattices. Individuals of one species can invade
a nearest-neighbor site in the lattice, while individuals of the other species
are able to invade sites at any distance but are less competitive locally,
i.e., they establish with a probability $g \le 1$. The model also accounts for
immigration, modeled as an external noise that may spontaneously replace an
individual at a lattice site by another individual of the other species. This
combination of mechanisms gives rise to a rich variety of outcomes for species
competition, including exclusion of either species, mono-stable coexistence of
both species at different population proportions, and bi-stable coexistence
with proportions of populations that depend on the initial condition.
Remarkably, in the bi-stable phase, the system undergoes a discontinuous
transition as the intensity of immigration overcomes a threshold, leading to a
half loop dynamics associated to a cusp catastrophe, which causes the
irreversible loss of the species with the shortest dispersal range.
Simultaneously, the immigration noise causes an increase in the difference on
the population proportions between the two species, which in turn is
compensated by the competition-dispersal tradeoff that ensures that the species
with the higher dispersal range has a larger share on the populations. Our model
provides a simple framework to explain the emergence of a half loop dynamics
and a discontinuous phase transition in spatial competition models, which is
constrained by regular lattices.

a half loop dynamics, a cusp catastrophe, and bi-stability, revealing how the

the first time, we provide a thorough analysis of the performance of the video
stream transcoding on heterogeneous cloud VMs. Providing such analysis is
crucial for efficient prediction of transcoding time on heterogeneous VMs and
for the functionality of any scheduling methods tailored for video transcoding.

of heterogeneous cloud VMs, in this research, we also provide a model to
quantify the degree of suitability of each cloud VM type for specific
transcoding tasks. The provided model can supply resource (VM) provisioning
methods with accurate performance and cost trade-offs to efficiently utilize
cloud services for video streaming.

property enables for accurate and seamless patch-wise reconstruction for some
important compressed sensing architectures.

larger than the state-of-the-art codes for video compressed sensing and
demosaicing, respectively. Detailed experimental evaluations show that those
codes also lead to reconstruction quality improvement (in terms of PSNR) of 0.7

media and nematic liquid crystals in a shear flow.

in spatial domains of different sizes. We find that these fluids can also move
coherently in domains of finite size, and the scaling behavior of the fluctuations in such systems is also determined.
  The hydrodynamic theory of the active fluids is obtained by linearizing the
stochastic Euler-Lagrange equation around a hydrodynamic velocity in time and
spatially. The same result is also obtained by a weak turbulence approach of
the Euler-Lagrange equation, which shows that the weak turbulence theory can
also be used to study these systems.

of the cuprates, we introduce the concept of
an "exceptional" van Hove singularity that appears when strong
electron-electron interaction splits an otherwise simply connected Fermi
surface into multiply connected pieces. The singularity describes the touching
of two pieces of the split Fermi surface. We show that this singularity is
proximate to a second order van Hove singularity, which can be accessed by
tuning a dispersion parameter. We argue that, in a wide class of cuprates, the
end-point of the pseudogap is accessed only by triggering the exceptional van
Hove singularity. The resulting Lifshitz transition is characterized by
enhanced specific heat and nematic susceptibility, as seen in experiments.
The exceptional van Hove singularity is also accessed in the presence of a
magnetic field, which explains the high field emergence of a pseudogap in
LSCO. Our theory provides a comprehensive explanation for the low energy
physics of the "stron-gap" pseudogap in cuprates.

a phonon field. We show that the exceptional van Hove singularity can be
activated by detuning the electron-phonon coupling from its ground state value.
This approach is relevant for transition metal oxides where phonons play an
important role. In cuprates, it can be used to explain the effect of
TiO$_2$ plane vibrations on the Fermi surface and the van Hove singularities.
The method provides a new approach to access the superconducting dome in
transition metal oxides and may be applied to other strongly interacting
systems, like the heavy fermion superconductors and the iron-based superconductors.

between superconductivity, and other order parameters, such as a nematic
state, that is caused by the electrons coupled to phonons.

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in orbit around small stars (M_* < 0.75 M_\odot).
  This sample represents a great complement to on-going and future RV
investigations of Kepler hosts, which will help constrain the effects of
stellar evolution on planetary systems.

additional products, including RV time series and planetary system models, are
available upon request.

the SEIR model that is capable of capturing the effect of events in a

ially private stochastic gradient
descent (DPSGD) is a fundamental challenge. Unlike the typical SGD, private
datasets cannot be used many times for hyperparameter search in DPSGD; e.g.,
via a grid search. Therefore, there is an essential need for algorithms that,
within a given search space, can find near-optimal hyperparameters for the best
achievable privacy-utility tradeoffs efficiently. We formulate this problem
into a general optimization framework for establishing a desirable
privacy-utility tradeoff, and systematically analyze three popular
hyperparameters (step size, batch size, and number of passes) and their impacts
on the tradeoff in the DPSGD. We observe that the problem of finding
hyperparameters is hard in general, and there is no general solution for these
dependencies. Therefore, we provide practical schemes that are tailored to
specific hyperparameters with justifiable analysis on their performance. Our
schemes significantly reduce the order of the number of required privacy
budgets compared to the sequential search. For example, finding the near-optimal
batch size requires $\log k$ privacy budgets (where $k$ is the number of grids
in the search space), while the sequential search requires $k$ budgets. We also
show how a small number of shadow models can accelerate our search significantly
via a utility-based early stopping criterion. Extensive experiments validate
our privacy-utility tradeoffs and show that our schemes significantly outperforms
the baseline baseline DPSGD in terms of both privacy and utility.
  As a byproduct of our analysis, we provide a privacy-utility benchmark against
which private learning algorithms that are not based on DPSGD should be evaluated.
We also propose a generic framework that allows us to compare the tradeoffs of
different private learning algorithms, making our framework useful in evaluating
and selecting the best private learning algorithms.
  We believe that our schemes for tuning the hyperparameters in DPSGD are
practical and can be widely applied, and our framework provides a general
framework for evaluating and comparing different private learning algorithms.
This framework can be utilized to study other aspects of private learning, e.g,
the tradeoff between privacy and communication cost in federated learning.

of 16 elemental
abundances in 34,410 Milky Way disk stars from the final data release (DR17) of
APOGEE-2. Building on recent work, we fit median abundance ratio trends [X/Mg]
vs. [Mg/H] with a 2-process model, which decomposes abundance patterns into a
"prompt" component tracing core collapse supernovae and a "delayed" component
tracing Type Ia supernovae. For each sample star, we fit the amplitudes of
these two components, then compute the residuals \Delta[X/H] from this
two-parameter fit. The rms residuals range from ~0.01-0.03 dex for the most
precisely measured APOGEE abundances to ~0.1 dex for Na, V, and Ce. The
correlations of residuals reveal a complex underlying structure, including a
correlated element group comprised of Ca, Na, Al, K, Cr, and Ce and a separate
group comprised of Ni, V, Mn, and Co. Selecting stars poorly fit by the
2-process model reveals a rich variety of physical outliers and sometimes
subtle measurement errors. Residual abundances allow comparison of populations
controlled for differences in metallicity and [\alpha/Fe]. Relative to the main
disk (R=3-13 kpc, |Z|<2 kpc), classical halo stars are overabundant in the
correlated element group and underabundant in the Ni, V, Mn, Co group; the reverse
holds for the young disk and for most intermediate- and high-iron peak elements
in the thick disk. The simple 2-process model captures ~80% of the mean
abundance ratio variations with [Mg/H] and provides a powerful tool for further
statistical analysis of APOGEE data and other spectroscopic surveys.
  Finally, we discuss potential applications and systematic limitations of this
analysis approach, which is unlikely to be widely adopted due to the computational
resources required. New pipelines utilizing more efficient algorithms and
capable of handling larger samples will have to be developed to fully explore
the power of APOGEE-2 (and future surveys) for quantitative studies of stellar
populations.
