Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic swept the
world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree
was suitable for predicting the peak coefficient, and the linear regression
model was ideal for predicting the attenuation coefficient. Our feature
analysis showed that precursor features were the most important for the
outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information
were the most important for the attenuation coefficient. Meanwhile, features
that were conducive to the outbreak were usually harmful to the continued
spread of rumors. At the same time, anxiety was a crucial rumor causing factor.
Finally, we discuss how to use deep learning technology to reduce the forecast
loss by combining the predicted values of the peak coefficient and attenuation
coefficient. The proposed method can help quantify rumors and cut down online
rumors effectively.

to their host galaxies thanks to the nearly universal shape of the planetary
nebulae luminosity function (PNLF). Accurate PNe distance measurements rely on
obtaining well-sampled PNLFs and the number of observed PNe scales with the
encompassed stellar mass. This means either disposing of wide-field
observations or focusing on the bright central regions of galaxies. In this
work we take this second approach and conduct a census of the PNe population in
the central regions of galaxies in the Fornax cluster, using VLT/MUSE data for
the early-type galaxies observed over the course of the Fornax3D survey. Using
such integral-field spectroscopic observations to carefully separate the
nebular emission from the stellar continuum, we isolated the [OIII] 5007 Å
emission component to create [OIII]-only images, and employed the latter to
identify PNe and construct PNe catalogues for 12 early-type galaxies. These
contain a total of almost 2800 PNe, with more than 1000 in the galaxy NGC
1386. We present the PNe catalogues, and after applying a variety of
quality-control steps, present the final derived PNLFs for each of the 12
galaxies, which are free from over-subtraction and contain no fills due to
underlying young star clusters. Combining these well-sampled PNLFs allows us
to create a new empirical distance estimator for early-type galaxies in the

systematic effects seen by previous works relying on the globular cluster luminosity

paper shows that currently available data processing solutions either fail to
meet the performance requirements or lack simple and flexible programming
interfaces. To address this problem, we propose \emph{LifeStream}, a
high-performance stream processing engine for physiological data. LifeStream
hits the sweet spot between ease of programming by providing a rich temporal
query language support and performance by employing optimizations that exploit
the periodic nature of physiological data. We demonstrate that LifeStream
achieves end-to-end performance up to $7.5\times$ higher than state-of-the-art
streaming engines and $3.2\times$ than hand-optimized numerical libraries on

better performance on large datasets than distributed solutions like HDFS and

workloads.

important hyperparameters for a
neural network. Many loss functions have been designed to date, making a
correct choice nontrivial. However, many sophisticated loss functions such as
the Relativistic Loss have been shown to outperform the simple Mean Squared
Error (MSE) loss only on very specific datasets. In this work, we design a
loss function that performs better than MSE across many datasets. Our method,
called Dense Comparative Loss (DCO), compares the input to the neural network
to a "dense comparator", a fully connected layer that is trained in parallel
to the rest of the network. We show that DCO performs better than MSE on a
very wide set of datasets, including both classification and regression
datasets, even when hyperparameters are tuned using a validation set. This is
the first loss function to date that demonstrates such performance.
  We also investigate why DCO performs better than other comparative loss
functions that have been previously designed. We observe that a recent
theoretical work by us [10] provides a comparative loss function design
framework, and that the success of DCO depends on the insights gained from this
framework. Our work shows that the comparative loss function design framework
proposed by us in [10] is generally powerful, and can be used to design many
other loss functions that also perform well.
  Finally, we demonstrate that DCO is robust to various attacks that try to
fool a comparison in DCO. This is interesting because DCO performs a
comparison of feature vectors, which is an explicit assumption that needs to
be made by the network (i.e. that there exists a dimension where the input
should be greater than/less than the target). That DCO can defend against
dimension-hopping attacks shows that DCO can learn a comparison that is
meaningful across various dimensions.
  In summary, in this work we design a comparison-based loss function that
performs better than MSE across very wide set of datasets, and also demonstrates
some interesting properties, such as being able to compare even after a
dimension-hopping attack.

the formation of coalescing black-hole (BH) - neutron-star (NS) binaries, such

investigate the effects of natal kicks and the NS's radius on the synthesis of
such systems and potential electromagnetic counterparts linked to them.
Synthetic models based on detailed core-collapse simulations result in an
increased merger detection rate of BH-NS systems ($\sim 2.3$ yr$^{-1}$), 5 to
10 times larger than the predictions of "standard" parametric prescriptions.
This is primarily due to the formation of low-mass BH via direct collapse, and
hence no natal kicks, favored by the detailed simulations. The fraction of
observed systems that will produce an electromagnetic counterpart, with the
detailed supernova engine, ranges from $2$-$25$%, depending on uncertainties in
the NS equation of state. Notably, in most merging systems with electromagnetic
counterparts, the NS is the first-born compact object, as long as the NS's
radius is $\lesssim 12\,\mathrm{km}$. Furthermore, core-collapse models that
predict the earliest collapse to a compact object (and hence the highest
birth mass) are preferentially those that yield merging systems with
counterparts.

consistently pairs core-collapse supernova models with compact binary evolution
and population synthesis. This is crucial to thoroughly investigate the link
between the two, as population synthesis assumes core-collapse models, but no
code exists that connects them directly so far.

preponderant effect in increasing the detection rate of merging BH-NS systems,
while core-collapse NSs contribute the most to the fraction of systems with
electromagnetic counterparts.

the study of compact binary mergers and their potential electromagnetic
counterparts, and demonstrates the usefulness of {\tt matchbox} in

following:

disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.
  - Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: We revisit the
information-theoretic one-time secure construction of Broadbent and Lord. The
success probability of the adversary in their construction was guaranteed to be
$0.85^n$, where $n$ is the length of the message. It was interesting to
understand whether the ideal success probability of (negligibly close to)

broader class of monogamy of entanglement games. We demonstrate a simple
cloning attack that succeeds with probability $0.71^n$ against a class of
schemes, showing a trade-off between the cryptographic criteria and the
computationally assumed hardness of the problem used in their construction.

security of the construction is based on the security of the underlying MPC
protocol) construction.

bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimisation problem that can be

that the performance of the resulting models exceeds that of models trained
with other common regularisers. We also provide evidence that the

define the $\mathcal{L}_2$ and $\mathcal{L}_p$ norm of a neural network,

technology to improve the detection of SLA Violations. We first describe the
principles of a P2P-based steering of active measurement mechanisms. These
principles are characterized by a meta-level that manages the measurement
probes, which can be seen as a P2P overlay node. These nodes cooperate to
measure the services by sending traffic between them and the service and
subsequently computing the performance. When a node detects a violation, the
meta-level is notified to activate reaction mechanisms. Second, we validate the
P2P measurement mechanism through an experimental study. The results show that the
mechanism can effectively detect SLA Violations compared to a centralized
mechanism. Third, we discuss and analyze potential challenges and opportunities

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios, further enlarging the application domain of imitation learning.
While various constraints have been studied, e.g., joint limits, obstacle
avoidance and plane constraints, the problem of nonlinear hard constraints has
not been well-addressed. In this paper, we propose extended kernelized movement
primitives (EKMP) to cope with most of the key problems in imitation learning,
including nonlinear hard constraints. Specifically, EKMP is capable of learning
the probabilistic features of multiple demonstrations, adapting the learned
skills towards arbitrary desired points in terms of joint position and
velocity, avoiding obstacles at the level of robot links, as well as satisfying
arbitrary linear and nonlinear, equality and inequality hard constraints.
Besides, the connections between kernelized movement primitives (KMP) and EKMP
are explicitly explained to provide comprehensive insights into imitation
learning. The efficacy of the proposed framework is demonstrated by five
scenarios, including the classic four-link robot arm scenario, planar chain
of seven holonomic joints, and their combinations with various nonlinear hard
constraints.

coupling in a Zeeman magnetic field provide a promising route to realize

fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here we use a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical
cluster approximation to study the superconducting properties of a doped
two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a
Zeeman magnetic field. We generally find that the Rashba coupling has a
beneficial effect towards s-wave superconductivity. In the presence of a finite
Zeeman field, when superconductivity is suppressed by Pauli pair-breaking, the
Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance created by the Zeeman field by
mixing the spins, and thus restores superconductivity at finite temperatures.
We show that this favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling is traced to a
spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of
electrons in time-reversed states. Moreover, by inspecting the Fermi surface of
the interacting model, we show that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and
Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to be topologically
non-trivial.
  Our results suggest that both the spin-orbit coupling and the Zeeman field
could be useful control parameters for realizing superconducting domains with
non-Abelian topological order in a material with Rashba coupling. Future
theoretical studies should investigate whether these conditions are met for
actual materials candidates.

pair-hopping amplitude and the temperature (or entropy). This has important
implications for the phase boundary between the two order parameters and the
tunneling behavior at low temperatures.

structure detection. We argue that these two applications are complementary to

dictatorship mechanism in social
choice settings, we explore its usefulness in tackling various combinatorial
optimization problems. We do so by considering an abstract model, in which a
set of agents are asked to act in a particular ordering, called the action
sequence. Each agent acts in a way that gives her the maximum possible value,
given the actions of the agents who preceded her in the action sequence. Our
goal is to compute action sequences that yield approximately optimal total
value to the agents (a.k.a., social welfare). We assume query access to the
value $v_i(S)$ that the agent i gets when she acts after the agents in the
ordered set $S$.
  We establish tight bounds on the social welfare that can be achieved using
polynomially many queries. Even though these bounds show a marginally sublinear
approximation of optimal social welfare in general, excellent approximations
can be obtained when the valuations stem from an underlying combinatorial
domain. Indicatively, when the valuations are defined using bipartite
matchings, arborescences in directed graphs, and satisfiability of Boolean
expressions, simple query-efficient algorithms yield $2$-approximations. We
discuss issues related to truthfulness and show how some of our algorithms can
be implemented truthfully using VCG-like payments. Finally, we introduce and
study the price of serial dictatorship, a new notion that captures the
excess cost of using a dictatorial mechanism, even when the agents take turns
to make the decisions.
  Our work opens the study of social welfare of serial dictatorial mechanisms
to combinatorial domains. It shows the importance of understanding the
performance of serial dictatorial mechanisms, since our investigation is
driven by a desire to optimize such mechanisms.

invariant channel matrices, the per-antenna transmit rate and the asymptotic

strongly depends on the regularization strength, and propose a tuning procedure
based on the characterizations offered. We also show that even if the
non-convex character of the Bayesian optimal processor hinders a meaningful
interpretation, its performance can be very close to the best possible, thus
setting a performance benchmark for other detection schemes.

Hamiltonian distance, and we derive efficient schemes to compute the optimal
regularization strength analytically, for the LASSO-type processors. We show
that these schemes significantly outperform plain cross-validation in a number of
high-frequency communication scenarios.

optimal detector, by exploiting its unitary-invariance property. We show that
this approach yields a significant improvement (up to 4 dB) of the error rate
performance, for medium to large values of $M$ and $N$.

various downstream tasks given limited labeled data. Among various methods,

positive and negative pairs. However, it is not trivial to build reasonable
pairs for a segmentation task in an unsupervised way. In this work, we propose
a novel unsupervised pre-training framework that avoids the drawback of
contrastive learning. Our framework consists of two principles: unsupervised

boundary-aware preserving learning. Experimental results on two benchmark
medical segmentation datasets reveal our method's effectiveness in improving
segmentation performance when few annotated images are available.

with full annotations. Therefore, our framework is a valuable unsupervised

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical metric between their knotoid distributions.
We detect geometric differences between trefoil proteins by characterising
their entanglement and we recover a clustering by sequence similarity. By
looking directly at the geometry and topology of their native states, we are
able to probe different folding pathways for proteins forming open-ended
trefoil knots. Interestingly, our pipeline reveals that the folding pathway of
shallow knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the creation of a double-looped
structure, differently from what was previously observed for deeply knotted
trefoil proteins. We validate this with Molecular Dynamics simulations.
Finally, our approach highlights that the formation of a double-looped structure
is not an artefact of the shallow depth of these knots, as it is also observed
in a non-native state of a deeply knotted protein. This work provides new
insights on the geometry and topology of trefoil proteins and suggests that the
present understanding of knotted proteins can be enhanced by analysing
knotoids.

universe, known as early dark
energy (EDE), is a proposed solution to the Hubble tension. Currently, there is
no consensus in the literature as to whether EDE can simultaneously solve the
Hubble tension and provide an adequate fit to the data from the cosmic
microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure of the universe. In this
work, we deconstruct the current constraints from the Planck CMB and the
full-shape clustering data of the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
(BOSS) to understand the origin of different conclusions in the literature. We
use two different analyses, a grid sampling and a component separation, to
investigate whether the current constraints suffer from volume effects upon
marginalization and are biased towards some values of the EDE fraction,
$f_\mathrm{EDE}$. We find that $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ allowed by the data strongly
depends on the particular choice of the other parameters of the model, and
different choices of these parameters lead to different modes in the
posterior. This suggests that the current constraints do pick out some values
of $f_\mathrm{EDE}$, and we are not seeing the full breadth of the EDE
component. We also observe that a more spread-out EDE component, which could
potentially better fit the data, is disfavored by the clustering data at
more than $2\sigma$, in agreement with previous studies. However, when we
add the early massive clusters data as an additional constraint, we find that
this conclusion may change as the fit to the EDE component marginally
improves when including this data.
  Finally, we discuss how the current analysis suffers from the lack of a
robust method to estimate the parameters of interest without assuming a
particular parametrization of the background and how this lack affects the
work already done on EDE and similar dark energy components in the early
universe. We argue that a more robust analysis is needed to investigate the
viability of EDE and eventually extract constraints on $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ that
are not biased by the choice of parametrization.
  We have made our code available open-source for further investigations of
EDE and possibly other early dark energy-like components at the following
GitHub link: https://github.com/AndreaRaccio/EDEmodule.

  The study of polymer flooding (polymer flooding is a process of injecting
polymers into oil reservoirs to increase the efficiency of oil extraction) is
motivated by the need to optimize the use of the polymers in the oil industry.
The model describing the process is given by a system of two partial
differential equations for the polymer and water concentrations in the porous
media. Due to the polymers' high cost, it is desirable to use as little as
possible while still efficiently increasing the viscosity of the fluid in the
porous media. This goal can be achieved by injecting polymers only in a few
"slugs" along the extraction pipe instead than continuously. This is why we
model the system considering a "tapering" strategy, i.e. slowly vanishing
injection profile. This is achievable both from a technological and
economical point of view, as it approximates, on the one hand, the case of
finite number of slugs (which is the most common practice) and it allows for a
significant gain of polymers (on the other hand). In this paper we present the
tapering strategy for a class of viscosity functions which includes the most
commonly used ones. We also consider the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models for
the mixing zones behavior, which are among the most used models in the industry
and can be considered as particular cases of the mixing zones models presented
in the book by Lake. In particular we prove that for the Koval model the
limiting polymer injection profile is of order $1/x$, while for the
Todd-Longstaff model it is exponential. Finally we present a numerical study
showing that the gain of polymers for the Koval model is of order $50\%$, while
for the Todd-Longstaff model it is of order $20\%$.

modeling the distribution of portfolio returns across portfolios. We establish
relevant mathematical formulas and propose efficient algorithms, drawing upon
powerful techniques in computational geometry and the literature on splines, to
compute the probability density function, the cumulative distribution function,
and the k-th moment of the probability function. Our algorithmic tools and
implementations efficiently handle portfolios with 10000 assets, and compute
moments of order k up to 40 in a few seconds, thus handling real-life
scenarios. We focus on the long-only strategy which is the most common type of
investment, i.e. on portfolios whose weights are non-negative and sum up to 1;
our approach is readily generalizable. Thus, we leverage a geometric
representation of the stock market, where the investment set defines a simplex
polytope. The cumulative distribution function corresponds to a portfolio score
capturing the percentage of portfolios yielding a return not exceeding a given
value. We introduce closed-form analytic formulas for the first 4 moments of
the cross-sectional returns distribution, as well as a novel algorithm to
compute all higher moments. We show that the first 4 moments are a direct
mapping of the asset returns' moments. All of our algorithms and solutions are
fully general and include the special case of equal asset returns, which was
sometimes excluded in previous works. Finally, we apply our portfolio score in
the specific context of equity markets, where it successfully captures the
cross-sectional distribution dynamics, and shows to be robust to noise and
overfitting.

real-world problems: an optimization problem with uncertain costs, a learning
problem on a social network, and an economic game involving strategic
decisions. In all three examples, the standardization transform provides
important insights that help to structure the problem and lead to better

wearable devices such as
smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare to tackle
these challenges. FedHealth performs data aggregation through federated
learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer learning. It is able
to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without compromising privacy
and security. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy
(5.3% improvement) for wearable activity recognition when compared to
traditional methods. FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential
to be used in many healthcare applications.

post-processing techniques. This is complicated due to the small number of
samples for such studies. Here, we present a supervised learning approach,
termed Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT). It learns a
supervised mapping of the temporal sequences onto a low dimensional grid. We
utilize a hidden markov model (HMM) to account for the time domain and
relevance learning to identify the relevant feature dimensions most predictive
over time. The learned mapping can be used to visualize the temporal sequences
and to predict the class of a new sequence. The relevance learning permits the
identification of discriminating masses or gen expressions and prunes
dimensions which are unnecessary for the classification task or encode mainly
noise. In this way we obtain a very efficient learning system for temporal
sequences. The results indicate that using simultaneous supervised learning and
metric adaptation significantly improves the prediction accuracy for
synthetically and realistically generated datasets.

multiple time points measured via Mass Spectrometry. This problem tries to
classify the nature of the samples at different time points. It has only 30
samples but 1200 features. This is a difficult problem, especially, for the
early stage of the experiment when many features might be unreliable. We
receive very promising results, especially, for the early stage of the
experiment. The analysis of this dataset tries to identify the major changes
occurred in p53 mutant cell lines over time and show how the SGTM-TT can help
a biologist in understanding and annotating her data.

efficiently analyze temporal sequences. It has applications in many domains,
and can help to answer many biological questions.

and the real dataset, the experimental setup and a thorough analysis of the

This problem studies the model where the same sequence from some set is
transmitted over multiple channels, and the decoder receives the different
outputs. Assume that the transmitted sequence is at distance $d$ from some code
and there are at most $r$ errors in every channel. Then the sequence
reconstruction problem is to find the minimum number of channels required to
recover exactly the transmitted sequence that has to be greater than the
maximum intersection between two metric balls of radius $r$, where the distance
between their centers is at least $d$. In this paper, we study the sequence
reconstruction problem of permutations under the Hamming distance. In this
model, we define a Cayley graph and find the exact value of the largest
intersection of two metric balls in this graph under the Hamming distance for
$r=4$ with $d\geqslant 5$, and for $d=2r$.
  Let $N(d,r)$ denote the size of the largest intersection of two metric balls
in this graph under the Hamming distance for which the distance between their
centers is at least $d$. The problem of finding $N(d,r)$ for arbitrary $d$ and
$r$ is an open problem. In 2008, A. Shtof and Z. Galil estimated $N(d,r)$ for
arbitrary $d$ and $r$. In particular, for $d=2r$, the estimate gives that
$N(2r, r)$ is at most $2^{(r-1)\log_2(5)+\delta(r)}$ for an arbitrary small
positive number $\delta(r)$. In this paper, for $d=2r$, we find the upper
bound of $N(2r,r)$, which is at most $2^{r\log_2(5)-\delta(r)}$, for some
positive number $\delta(r)$.

the different regimes arising from this competition. However, they exploit
wavefunctions relying on crystal band symmetries, which tunneling interactions

tunneling coupling through the shared crystallographic plane, which is
insensitive to the dopants wavefunction symmetry and has a simpler dependence on
distance. The on-site alignment is preserved in the presence of lattice
decoherence, and it should be generally observable for any atomically placed

summarizing the unstructured data does not help LLMs perform better on the

structured representation, whereas the variance leads to better performance of
LLMs on the structured knowledge query task. To support our argument, we
propose a framework to evaluate the variance of knowledge extracted from
unstructured data by LLMs relative to the structured representation. We show
that the framework reveals the significance of the variance, which further
improves the performance of LLMs on the structured knowledge query task.

LLMs to encode the knowledge in a way that is easily query-able. To support our
claim, we show that even small-sized LLMs trained on the structured data

the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In contrast, a more sophisticated multiple-fluid model predicts a broad
distribution of fluxes, with a long tail of negative flux in the strongly
buoyant regime. This suggests that a multiple-fluid model is not sufficient to
represents the strong coherence of overturning structures in convection.
However, the overall magnitude of the flux is still accurately predicted,
suggesting that a multi-fluid model might be able to predict a correct model
scale heat flux when closed in a more comprehensive atmospheric model.
  We argue that a two-fluid model is the simplest framework that can capture
the strong coherence of overturning structures that is a hallmark of turbulent
convection. This suggests that as more is learned about closing a two-fluid
model, this might be the most attractive multi-scale convection scheme for
atmospheric models.

provides a direct diagnostic of the level of coherence in a flow. Traditionally
the level of coherence (e.g. in the form of vertical velocity correlations)

evidence for the greater coherence of two-fluid from that of a multi-fluid
simulation.

rotating partitions create a horizontal shear in temperature that creates a

CMS) detector is one of two general-purpose
detectors that measure the products of high energy particle interactions in the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. The silicon pixel detector is the
innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in
operation between 2009 and 2016 has now been replaced with an upgraded one in
the beginning of 2017. During the previous shutdown period of the LHC, a
prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.
  Given the successful performance testing of the new modules with cosmic ray
data, the CMS pixel detector upgrade is well-prepared for the operation with
the LHC at its design luminosity in 2022.
  Based on data recorded in 2015-2018, the track residual distributions are
shown to confirm the expected improvement in the hit resolution due to the
increased segmentation in the new modules.
  The hit residual distributions indicate an improvement in the hit resolution
from 8 to 6 pix (pix = 436 $\mu$m), where pix is the pixel size in the new
modules.
  The performance of the new modules is good and ready for the LHC operation
with a hit residual distribution width consistent with the design specification
of less than 7 pix.
  The good performance indicates that the quality of the modules is consistent
with the requirements for the new detector modules.
  The good performance in cosmic rays and satisfactory in pp data indicate that
the new digital read-out chips and front-end drivers work well and are ready
for the LHC operation.
  In summary, the test of the hit finding and track reconstruction using the
new modules confirms that the new detector modules are operational and ready
for the LHC data-taking with a good hit resolution.
  This underlines the success of the detector upgrade program and shows that the
new detector modules meet the design specifications.
  Finally, it is important to note that the good performance of the new modules
is also important for future uprating of the computing system of the CMS
detector

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  We propose ranking farmers based on their entire density functions of
strawberry fruit production rather than just their average values. We use a
density-based method using kernel density estimation and propose using the
number of trials as a surrogate variable to control for the trial effects. We
apply this methodology to simulate the density functions of fruit production
for the treatment and control groups. Our results show that this density-based
approach provides higher statistical power compared to the stochastic efficiency
approach. We also find that the disease pressure has a positive impact on the
mean but a negative impact on the median of the yield and profit, suggesting
that the high levels of disease pressure are detrimental to the fruit
production.
  Farmers make decisions based on their entire density functions rather than
just their averages. A density-based approach provides higher statistical
power than a frontier approach when the number of observations is limited.
Using a density function allows us to capture the heterogeneity of production
and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield and profit.
Including the effect of disease pressure provides a more general framework to
evaluate pesticide efficacy and allows us to draw stronger conclusions about
the pest management strategies that should be adopted by farmers, especially
those in areas with high disease pressures.

weak equivalence principle (WEP) is based on
the minute measurement of the difference of accelerations experienced by two
test masses as they orbit the Earth. A detection of a violation of the WEP
would appear at a well-known frequency $f_{\rm EP}$ depending on the
satellite's orbital and spinning frequencies. Consequently, the experiment was
optimised to miminise systematic errors at $f_{\rm EP}$. Glitches are
short-lived events visible in the test masses' measured acceleration, most
likely originating in cracks of the satellite's coating. In this paper, we
characterise their shape and time distribution. Although intrinsically random,
their time of arrival distribution is modulated by the orbital and spinning
periods. They have an impact on the WEP test that must be quantified. However,
the data available prevents us from unequivocally tackling this task. We show
that glitches affect the test of the WEP, up to an a priori unknown level.
Discarding the perturbed data is thus the best way to reduce their effect.
Finally, we estimate the improved sensitivity that will be gained by doing so.
Removing all glitches above 10$^{-7}$~m/s would increase the mission's
sensitivity by a factor of about four.

based on the determination of the satellite's centre of mass. The method
provides a direct way to take into account the effects of the perturbing
moments on the test of the WEP. It was developed specifically for the
MICROSCOPE mission, but it is applicable to any such mission.

on-board accuracy was remarkably high, reducing the standard deviation of the
satellite's acceleration measurement to less than 2~10$^{-8}$~g. As a result,
the final analysis of the experiment is not limited by the instrument's
performance, but only to a level of 5~10$^{-8}$. Moreover, a detailed study
of the perturbations shows that a gain of an order of magnitude in sensitivity
can be reached by improving the modelling of the satellite's orbit and magnetic
environment, and by reducing the effects of the perturbbing moments generated
by the solar wind and the radiation

both the student and teacher networks are trained in conjunction on the same

temperature scaling assumption in KD. We show both theoretically and
empirically that the choice of temperature in KD is an important factor, with
which the same student network could yield significantly different performance
under different teaching (softmax) temperatures. With this observation, we
propose to treat the temperature as a "free parameter" in KD, and achieve
significant acceleration (up to 17x) and reduction in model size (up to 1/128)

distillation framework. Our code is available at:

not converge under traditional KD.

deep networks without any distillation. Our analysis shows that TR is
surprisingly effective in improving network performance and enabling model
size reduction.

modifiiction of Stanley's method based on the composition factors of $M$. As

human experts can be expensive to obtain in large numbers. On the other hand,
it is often much easier to obtain large quantities of suboptimal or
task-agnostic trajectories, which are not useful for direct imitation, but can
nevertheless provide insight into the dynamical structure of the environment,

to facilitate provably improved downstream imitation learning? In this work, we
answer this question affirmatively and present training objectives that use
offline datasets to learn a factored transition model whose structure enables
the extraction of a latent action space. Our theoretical analysis shows that
the learned latent action space can boost the sample-efficiency of downstream
imitation learning, effectively reducing the need for large near-optimal expert
datasets through the use of auxiliary non-expert data. To learn the latent
action space in practice, we propose TRAIL (Transition-Reparametrized Actions
for Imitation Learning), an algorithm that learns an energy-based transition
model contrastively, and uses the transition model to reparametrize the action
space for sample-efficient imitation learning. We evaluate the practicality of
our objective through experiments on a set of navigation and locomotion tasks.
Our results verify that, with moderate quantities of suboptimal offline data,
TRAIL can improve the sample-efficiency of upstream imitation learning, reducing
the need for large near-optimal expert datasets by one order of magnitude.
Furthermore, we observe that TRAIL can also improve the performance of models
trained with large near-optimal expert datasets, reducing the need for large

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news domains, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.
  In particular, our analysis brings three novel contributions. First, it
defines a novel metric for measuring polarization, namely polarization of
browsing time. Second, it shows how such a metric can be utilized in order to
disentangle the role of hyperlink structure versus homogeneous preferences
from the emergence of online polarization. Third, it provides a robust
methodology for addressing issues arising from the intrinsic complexity of the
Web, namely issues related to extrinsic factors as well as issues related to
Web scraping.
  Overall, the proposed approach offers a versatile methodology which can be
deployed in order to study the role of the Web in the societal problem of
polarization as well as other problems involving the interaction of humans and
the Web.

well-characterized and rich case study of polarization, which can be utilized
in order to draw further insights and inform future studies.

which can be utilized in order to study the role of Web systems in the
development of polarization as well as other societal problems.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.

the problem to finding good quantizers for the functions $x\mapsto \|x-x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)}$.

a multi-agent
system where a fraction of the agents act in an adversarial manner.
Specifically, the malicious agents steer the network of agents away from the
optimal solution by sending false information to their neighbors and consume
significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one another. We prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, and characterize the
solutions obtained under the communication-constrained environment and presence
of malicious agents. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are also
presented.

a quantity of malicious agents as a fraction of the total number of agents, as
done in [14] is not feasible to implement in a multi-agent system. Further,
the existing literature, e.g., [5, 17], considers a scenario in which only
malicious agents transmit false information to their neighbors in a network,
 whereas in many practical problems, all agents including malicious ones may
transmit false information with the false information being different in each
transmission. Finally, in many multi-agent systems, e.g., sensor networks,
agents are of different capabilities; see e.g., [16]. Our proposal addresses
the problem of optimizing a objective function defined over the space of
agents with respect to the leader agent under the communication constraints
between the leader and other agents and in presence of malicious agents.

low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume that the degree distributions of
the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, increasing
the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error
protection (UEP) design.

means for unconditional secure key
transmission between two distant parties. However, in practical
implementations, it suffers from quantum hacking due to device imperfections.
Here we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, homodyne
detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy
state QKD system when the phase of source is partially randomized. Our analysis
shows that, in some parameter regimes, the proposed attack would result in an
entanglement breaking channel but still be able to trick the legitimate users
to believe they have transmitted secure keys. That is, the eavesdropper is able
to steal all the key information without discovered by the users. Thus, our
proposal reveals that partial phase randomization is not sufficient to
guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems with weak coherent states.
Our study further emphasizes the need of a rigorous security analysis on any
QKD systems that could be implemented in the future.
  We also propose another trick that makes the hybrid attack even more
practical. That is, we propose a pre-filter to the transmitter to reduce the
amount of state to be attacked. Surprisingly, our analysis shows that this
completely does not affect the final key transmission rate, but significantly
simplifies the analysis. That is, our proposal reveals that the conventional
state reduction technique could improve the key transmission rate at the cost
of the complexity of the analysis.
  Our studies further emphasize the necessity of strictly proof-checking the
security of QKD systems before any practical implementations.
  Finally, we show that the proposed attacks would not work if the source is
fully phase randomized. That is, our proposals do illustrate the importance of
randomizing the phase of source in practice.
  We conclude that the proposed hybrid attack scheme illustrates the
importance of strictly proof-checking the security of any QKD systems before
any practical implementations.

from traditional resource allocation mechanisms as Base Stations (BSs) will be
empowered with computation capabilities (i.e., offloading and computation is

resource management, within the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) paradigm, we
make use of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network for time series
forecasting and control-theoretic techniques for foresighted optimization, thus
bringing intelligent mechanisms for handling network resources within the
network edge. Here, historical traffic load measurements are used as input to
the LSTM network to predict future traffic loads for different regions of the
network. Then, online optimization mechanisms, which leverage the predicted
traffic loads, are employed to determine on-the-fly the number of computations
offloaded to the MEC server of each BS, and also to allocate spectrum and
allocate power for the uplink communications of the MN. This combination of
prediction and optimization enables the determination of near-optimal
throughput for all users, reduces offloading latency, and also improves the
energy efficiency of the MN. The proposed approach is evaluated through
simulation, where the cooperative optimization of offloading and spectrum
allocation is compared to a non-cooperative scenario in which these two issues
are addressed independently, and also to a scenario in which we only offload
but then address the spectrum allocation through a decentralized mechanism. The
results reveal that the cooperative scenario, which solves for offloading and
spectrum allocation jointly, yields the best performance in terms of
throughput, energy, and offloading latency, achieving an increase of 2x, 1.5x, and
10x, respectively, when compared to the two other scenarios. Also, the proposed
scheme is deployed in an real testbed environment using MinION and ERTRA
tools. The results show that our scheme achieves an increase in throughput of
20% and a decrease in offloading latency of 30% compared to the baseline
solution. From this work it is possible to conclude that the use of MEC and
intelligent resource management can bring important benefits to the future MNs
and also to the overall society, as it enables efficient processing and data
transmission at the network edge

angle function. He introduced a general definition of this notion for metric
and semi-metric spaces. He also proposed two problems concerning conformal
embeddability of spaces endowed with an angle function into Euclidean spaces.
These problems received attention in later years but only for some particular
cases of metric spaces. We show that conformal embeddability into the Euclidean
space of dimension 3 (resp. 2) is equivalent to the existence of an angle
function if the space is a certain kind of 3-dimensional (resp. 2-dimensional)
space. In this way we solve the first Menger's problem for the dimension 3 and
completely the second one.

$\mathcal{G}$-convex if for every pair of points $x,y \in S$ the unique geodesic
segment (for the gauge $\mathcal{G}$) joining $x$ to $y$ is contained in $S$.

  In finite systems a transformation to represent the electromagnetic radiation
by the electric field instead is possible, albeit subtleties arise in periodic
systems. The resulting dipole gauge is a multi-orbital generalization of
Peierl's substitution. In this work, we investigate accuracy of both pathways,
with particular emphasis on gauge invariance, for TB models constructed from
maximally localized Wannier functions. Focusing on paradigmatic two-dimensional
materials, we construct first-principle models and calculate the response to
electromagnetic fields in linear response and for strong excitations.
Benchmarks against fully converged first-principle calculations allow for
ascertaining the accuracy of the TB models. We find that the dipole gauge
provides a more accurate description than the velocity gauge in all cases. The
main deficiency of the velocity gauge is an imperfect cancellation of
paramagnetic and diamagnetic current. Formulating a corresponding sum rule
however provides a way to explicitly enforce this cancellation. This procedure
corrects the TB models in the velocity gauge, yielding excellent agreement with
dipole gauge and thus gauge invariance.
  Our study provides a comprehensive guideline for constructing accurate
first-principle TB models. It further opens the door for investigating
light-matter interaction in artificial systems constructed from TB models, where
the dipole gauge is preferred. As example, we investigate photoionization of
helium in a TB model using either the dipole gauge or the velocity gauge with
paramagnetic-diamagnetic cancellation. Both approaches give the same result, but
the latter yields a regular instead of a singular photoionization spectrum.
This regularization points to a fundamental aspect of photoionization, namely
the coupling to electromagnetic modes created by the ionized electron.
Importantly, this phenomenon is not contained in the dipole gauge.

investigating optical and strong-field phenomena in solids and molecules. With
two simple tricks -- using the dipole gauge or enforcing the cancellation of
paramagnetic and diamagnetic current in the velocity gauge -- their accuracy can
be substantially increased.

node can be connected to itself in order to avoid the loss of relevant
information. This is particularly important in the context of Boolean functions,
as the selfconnections can play a crucial role in determining the behaviour of
a node. It is then clear that one needs to be able to treat the selfconnections
in a proper way in order to be able to study systems with self-interactions.

generalise the cavity method to systems that are driven out of equilibrium by

the framework of generative adversarial networks (GANs) since the entire

suffer from unreliable gradient estimations or imprecise sentence
representations. Inspired by the principle of sparse coding, we propose a
SparseGAN that generates semantic-interpretable, but sparse sentence
representations as inputs to the discriminator. The key idea is that we treat
an embedding matrix as an over-complete dictionary, and use a linear
combination of very few selected word embeddings to approximate the output
feature representation of the generator at each time step. With such
semantic-rich representations, we not only reduce unnecessary noises for
efficient adversarial training, but also make the entire training process fully
differentiable. Experiments on multiple text generation datasets yield

mission planning of
unmanned aerial system swarms. Given a swarm operating in a known area, a
central command system generates measurements from the swarm. If those
measurements indicate changes to the mission situation such as target movement,
the swarm planning is updated to reflect the new situation and guidance updates
are broadcast to the swarm. The primary algorithms featured in this work are A*
pathfinding and the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli multi-target tracking
method.
  To evaluate this technique, a simulation environment was built to simulate
the described swarm mission planning process. In the environment, a swarm
operates to track multiple targets. The tracker runs on the simulation and is
tuned during runtime. After the mission, the simulation analyzes the mission
through quantitative metrics.
  The results show that the proposed swarm planning technique effectively
supports the tracking of multiple targets. The use of a centralized tracker
allows the planner to make informed decisions during mission execution. In
particular, the combination of A* and GLMB enables the swarm to quickly
adapt to changing situations.
  Further analysis shows that the performance of the swarm depends on the
wavelength used by the swarm's sensors. This is a prime example for the need
for wavelength diversity in swarm design. This finding suggests that swarms
operating in an urban area should use sensors with short wavelengths such as
infrared or laser to navigate and track targets, while avoiding areas with
reflective surfaces or strong interference.
  Finally, the proposed simulation environment allows the analysis of swarm
missions in various scenarios. It can be used to compare different
multitarget tracking algorithms and pathfinding methods.
  In summary, the described algorithm and simulation environment show that the
proposed swarm planning process allows the effective mission execution of a
multi-UAS system. The use of A* and GLMB enables the swarm to quickly adapt to
changing situations, and the simulation allows the analysis and comparison of
different algorithms and scenarios.
  Future work will focus on the implementation of the proposed algorithms in
an experimental setting and the analysis of mission scenarios modeled from
real-world video footage.

information from historical form images. Historical forms are varied in layout
and contain degraded text. Handwritten input text can be difficult to read or
missed altogether. Pre-printed text can be small or similar in appearance to
handwritten text. A crucial step in extracting information from historical forms

template-free approach to this sub-task and show that our approach is effective

problem when prompting. We show that by simply splitting the input into

architecture becomes capable of understanding the context within the entire
input. This method is particularly effective when the input is very long, and
it has similar parameter efficiency compared to multi-task prompting. We also
show that by adding entities as implicit arguments to the prompts, the
architecture becomes capable of understanding the logical relationship between
the entities and generating more coherent and relevant responses. Finally, we
show that by using conditional prompting, the architecture can generate
differently conditioned on the same input. For example, the architecture can
generate both positively and negatively polarized responses for the same text.

language processing tasks that require long context and multiple entities.

on the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition, in which
instead of solving the Hamiltonian constraint as a 2nd order elliptic equation
for a choice of mean curvature $K$, we solve an algebraic equation for $K$ for
a choice of conformal factor. By doing so, we evade the existence and
uniqueness problem of solutions of the Hamiltonian constraint without using the
usual conformal rescaling of the source terms. This is particularly important
when the sources are fundamental fields, as reconstructing the fields'
configurations from the rescaled quantities is potentially problematic. Using
an iterative multigrid solver, we show that this method provides rapid
convergent solutions for several initial conditions that have not yet been
studied in numerical relativity; namely (i) periodic inhomogeneous spacetimes
with large random Gaussian scalar field perturbations and (ii) asymptotically
flat black hole spacetimes with rotating scalar clouds.

conformal factor which significantly improves the rate of convergence of the
iteration. In addition, we show how one can decompose the Maxwell part of a
multi-component fluid into transverse and longitudinal parts, which then allows
us to apply the CTT decomposition to the fluids' tensors. Finally, we record
several new scalar quantities that measure the magnitude of the fluids' flows
in different ways, one of which we use to study the behavior of the fluids in
the spacetimes formed in (i) and (ii) above.

typically treated as sources that contribute to the stress tensor of the

the underlying theory of general relativity, which does not allow for a

optimization problems whose solutions are embedded into a ground state of the

the driver Hamiltonian to the problem Hamiltonian, we can obtain the target
ground state that corresponds to the solution. The inclusion of non-stoquastic
terms in the driver Hamiltonian is believed to enhance the efficiency of the
QA. Meanwhile, decoherence is regarded as of the main obstacles for QA. Here,
we present examples showing that non-stoaquastic Hamiltonians can lead to
catastrophic failure of QA, whereas a certain decoherence process can be used
to avoid such failure. More specifically, when we include anti-ferromagnetic
interactions (i.e., typical non-stoquastic terms) in the Hamiltonian, we are
unable to prepare the target ground state even with an infinitely long
annealing time for some specific cases. In our example, the ground state that
we actually obtain by QA is a symmetry-related state that does not correspond
to the target ground state. Moreover, we show that, in certain cases, we can
obtain the target ground state, but with a macroscopically degenerate
Hamiltonian. In such a case, we can use a macroscopically degenerate state as
a intermediate state in QA, and thereby obtain the target ground state
efficiently. This suggests that decoherence can be used to activate a
Hamiltonian that has only a non-degenerate ground state, and thus allows us to
prepare the target ground state that we are seeking. We also show that we can
use a macroscopically degenerate Hamiltonian as a final state in QA, and
thereby obtain a target ground state that is related to the macroscopically
degenerate state. This suggests that we can map a macroscopically degenerate
Hamiltonian to a target problem Hamiltonian by using QA.

different outcomes of QA: namely, catastrophic failure and enhancement of the
efficiency of QA. The possibility of using decoherence in QA is also interesting

to obtain by QA.

ofiller-modified polymer matrices have
immense potential to improve the safety of high-risk engineering structures.
These materials are intrinsically self-sensing because their electrical
conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites which can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, that are difficult to
detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
determining damage shape and size in self-sensing composites. Our technique
makes use of a genetic algorithm (GA) integrated with realistic physics-based
damage models to recover precise damage shape from conductivity changes imaged
via EIT. We experimentally validate this technique on carbon nanofiber
(CNF)-modified glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates by considering
two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. Our results
show that this novel technique can accurately reconstruct multiple
through-holes with radii as small as 1.5 mm and depths up to 50% of the
laminates' thickness. Furthermore, our technique has successfully reimaged a
complex delamination defect, demonstrating that it has great potential for
reconstructing more complex real-world damage.

students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Two statistics are used for comparison:
mean comparison using t-test and proportion comparison using z-test. The
latter is used for examining the percentage indicators. Both statistics are
applied at a significance level of 0.05. The results show that remote learning
has a negative impact on transfer students' ability to engage with learning
modules, and also has a negative impact on first generation students' ability
to submit modules early for extra credit. The results are discussed in the
context of the extra challenges that undergraduate transfer students and first
generation college students face during the COVID-19 pandemic, and how online
learning may exacerbate these challenges.

statistics for each network generated in an iteration. From the statistics, we
observe that some generators produce networks with the same topological
summary statistics profile while other generators produce different topological
profiles even at the same level of reticulations. We argue that topological

than the lattice spacing, the topological parameters will directly scale with
the correlation length. (ii) If the correlation length is of the same order as
the lattice spacing, the topological phases will emerge only when there is a

collisions is sensitive to initial and final state interactions in the
medium-classical parton scattering and parton-medium interactions. By studying
the hadron distribution at large angles to direct photons, we access the
information carried by the photons about the initial-state geometry and
interactions. In particular, the hadron distribution at small hadron $p_T$ is
expected to be sensitive to the initial-state geometry fluctuations.

deployment of HPC workloads on the best-fitting hardware. However, although
cloud and on-premise HPC systems offer similar computational resources, their
network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the
application scaling. This work analyzes network performance, scalability, and
cost of running HPC workloads on cloud systems. First, we consider latency,
bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we consider the one-dimensional
Tonks-Hohenberg Bose gas and study the effective description of the
Hamiltonian that emerges in the matrix product density matrix (MPDM) approach,
which is a powerful tool for simulating quantum dynamics of interacting
many-body systems. We show that the outcome of an annealing process can be
predicted from the outcome of a quench by identifying the "effective" coupling
constant that describes the annealing process in the same way that the
"effective" coupling constant describes the quench. On the level of the
Hamiltonian, this connection can be made explicit by introducing a "effective"
Hamiltonian that describes the annealing process. This suggests that the
connection between quench and annealing can be exploited in practical
applications to speed up annealing protocols.
  From a theoretical perspective, the connection between quench and annealing
is interesting because it suggests that the strong-time-dependent perturbation
theory, which is used to describe the quench dynamics, can be extended to
describe annealing dynamics.
  Our work is a first step in making this connection for any quantum system.
However, in practice, the relation between quench and annealing will depend on
the specific system under investigation and on the level of approximation used
to describe the dynamics.
  In particular, in order to talk about the "effective" Hamiltonian, we need
to identify a conserved quantity, like the total momentum, that allows us to
describe the dynamics in a momentum sector where the Hamiltonian is
diagonal.
  In systems with no global symmetries, like the one studied in this work, a
coarse-graining on a lattice is required to obtain a Hamiltonian that has a
conserved quantity, like the "momentum" of the effective Hamiltonian.
  Furthermore, in order to talk about annealing, we need to include a
parametric change of the Hamiltonian that is slow enough to explore
equilibrium phases.
  Then, the "effective" Hamiltonian will provide us with the information on
which equilibrium phase we are in during the annealing process.

as a sum of squares has a
long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some
specific rings (like integers or polynomials over the rationals), there are
known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for
many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of an
arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.
  Our approach is based on recent advances in the theory of global fields, like
the denomination of Gaussians in the function field case, and the theory of
Minkowski-type results involving Gaussian measures on the ring of integers of
a number field. We show that every element of the ring of an arbitrary global
field has a decomposition of length at most 4 into a sum of squares. This result
is effectively computable using modern computer algebra systems, like SageMath.
We demonstrate the power and efficiency of this algorithm by generating large
tables of decompositions of squares into sums of squares for various global
fields, starting from relatively small fields (like quadratic or biquadratic
fields) up to larger families of fields (like the family of fields ${\mathbb
Q}(\root{n}{2}, \root{m}{2})$ for various $n$ and $m$).
  Finally, we show how a carefully optimized version of our algorithm can be
implemented to compute large tables of decompositions for the field ${\mathbb
Q}(\root{127}{2})$. The largest table that we were able to compute (with
approximately $5\cdot 10^8$ elements) weighs about 24 GB and contains over
650,000 distinct squares with a decomposition of length 4. This database is
available online at https://github.com/MHail602/DeMoS2.
  We hope that this database will be useful for future mathematical
investigations. We also point out that it is relatively easy to implement a
web-interface to this database, which could be made available online, for
example, as a web-service, which could answer questions like "What are all the
squares in ${\mathbb Q}(\root{127}{2})$ which can be written as a sum of 4
squares?".

the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has shown to worsen with increasing local
updates. In this work, we propose a family of algorithms that enable model
learning without increasing the variance due to data heterogeneity, even as
more local updates are employed. Our approach relies on a novel formulation of
the Federated Learning problem that highlights the role of the local updates as
a form of distributed quantization. Based on this new formulation, we design a
family of algorithms that include as special cases some of the most popular
optimization and learning algorithms, such as Federated Averaging (FA), Federated
Optimization (FO), and Non-Convex Constrained Optimization (NCCO), as well as
a novel algorithm called Homogenizing Local Updates (HLU) that enjoys a lower
variance than its counterparts. We show that all the algorithms in the HLU
family enjoy communication complexity bounds that are linear in the number of
nodes and logarithmic in the desired accuracy, improving upon the best known
bounds in the literature. Our work is the first to show that optimal communication
complexity bounds can be achieved in FL problems that involve minimization over
a convex set even when the data are statistically heterogeneous and only a
small number of iterations are employed.

affected by the rotation in the turbulence.

complex local atomic structure and coarse-grained materials phenomena.

based on this competition is consistent with the experimental failure patterns.

an order parameter that characterizes spatial correlations in the rift
formation. We measure the correlation function of the cluster length and
quantitatively show that rifts are correlated over a large number of particles

lead to a cluster-effect in the average cluster length, which qualitatively
explains the failure modes observed in experiments at high pulling velocities.

correlation effect, and the intrinsic velocity dependence of the cluster length
can be observed.

standard normal. We illustrate our findings in drawing inference on the suicide
rate before and after the emergency, where we derive expressions for the
asymetric distribution of the difference between two rounded averages.

multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step

However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, and thus the trained
policy has a suboptimal performance. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL
from the perspective of reward decomposition (RD) and propose a novel framework
called Reward Decomposition for Offline Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
(RD-MARL) that allows an agent to benefit from the rewards generated by its
neighbors. By decomposing the global reward into local rewards based on the
graph structure of the multi-agent system, RD-MARL enables each agent to
optimize its policy using the local rewards independently, and thus an agent
can get a optimal policy regardless of the behavior policy of its neighbors.

environments, and the results show that RD-MARL significantly outperforms the
state-of-the-art offline MARL algorithms.

  Federated Learning (FL) is a privacy-preserving learning paradigm that allows
multiple organizations to collaborate on building a common machine learning
model without gathering the actual training data. However, the limited data
available at each organization (i.e., client) may lead to a model that is not
effective enough for use in practice. One way to build a more effective model
is to add external data sourced from other sources without permission or
oversight, which may compromise the privacy and security of the clients' data.
To address this issue, we propose a novel FL framework that enables the
collaborative training of models using private datasets while allowing for the
relatively public data of a global expert to be incorporated without violating
the privacy of the clients' data. Our framework ensures that the clients'
private data do not leave the local devices and only the aggregated data
contributed by all the clients are used to update the global model. We show
that our framework is more efficient than the traditional FL in terms of
training a model that achieves comparable performance on a public dataset. We
also show that our framework outperforms a baseline method that incorporates
public data into the FL without any modifications. Our experiment results show
that the models obtained using our framework achieve up to 10% higher accuracy
and up to 21% higher F1-score compared to the baseline method.

literature, as the major medium that carries knowledge between scientists,
exhibits explosive growth during the last century. Despite the frequent use of
many tangible measures, such as citation, impact factor and g-index, to
quantify the influence of papers from different perspectives based on
scientific productivity, it has not yet been well understood how the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By
leveraging Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon
entropy in unstructured probability space, we propose the Quantitative Index of
Knowledge (KQI), which is taken as the subtraction between the two types of
entropy, to reflect the extent of disorder of the system, how the knowledge
accumulates and how the knowledge value of each article is determined. The
analysis on 19 major scientific areas reveals that the knowledge amount in most
disciplines is not the highest in the place where productivity is the highest,
except for physics and, interestingly, the knowledge amount in the place where
the productivity is the second highest is often the highest. Our findings provide
new perspectives on the understanding of the understanding of the knowledge
accumulation in various scientific areas and provide unique insights into the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount. It is hoped
that our findings can provide useful references for further scientific
discoveries and help policymakers make informed decisions about scientific
investment based on our quantitative index of knowledge.
