layer security (PLS) problem in the dual
hop orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) based wireless
communication system. First, we consider a single user single relay system and
study a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay subject to
individual power constraint at the two nodes. The aim is to maximize the end to
end secrecy rate with optimal power allocation over different sub-carriers.
Later, we consider a more general multi-user multi-relay scenario. Under high
SNR approximation for end to end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is
formulated to jointly optimize power allocation at the BS, the relay selection,
sub-carrier assignment to users and the power loading at each of the relaying
node. The target is to maximize the overall security of the system subject to
independent power budget limits at each transmitting node and the OFDMA based
exclusive sub-carrier allocation constraints. A joint optimization solution is
obtained through duality theory. Dual decomposition allows to exploit convex
optimization techniques to find the power loading at the source and relay
nodes. Further, an optimization for power loading at relaying nodes along with
relay selection and sub carrier assignment for the fixed power allocation at
the BS is also studied. Lastly, a sub-optimal scheme that explores joint power
allocation at all transmitting nodes for the fixed subcarrier allocation and
relay assignment is investigated. Finally, simulation results show the
effectiveness of the proposed approaches to improve the security of the dual
hop OFDM based wireless communication system.

correlations at strong exchange fields, affecting the detailed character of the
proximity effect. We show that the magnetic control of the spin-valve behavior

orientation-dependent averaging mechanism of the magnetic inhomogeneity on the

factors provide one general way to compare different hypotheses by their
compatibility with the observed data. Those quantifications can then also be
used to choose between hypotheses. While Bayes factors provide an immediate
approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a tool for Bayesian inferences and
discuss that utility functions are needed for principled decisions on
hypotheses. Next, we study how Bayes factors misbehave under different
conditions. This includes a study of errors in the estimation of Bayes factors.
Importantly, it is unknown whether simple guidelines can be given for when to
use Bayes factors versus other approaches to parameter estimation and
hypothesis testing. We therefore investigated a wide range of settings in
which Bayes factors are used and studied how those settings can be improved by
utilizing MCMC posterior inference more directly. We discuss that utility
functions are vital for Bayes factor analyses, but also that MCMC based
approaches can be made more robust by employing techniques from the field of
statistical analysis of frequentist tests. Finally, we explain how to encode
the results of Bayes factor analyses in a way that is useful for decisions by
using Bayes Decisions Tables. This is important because even when Bayes
factors are calculated properly, the results can be difficult to translate
into decisions. Together these guidelines can help to make Bayes factor
analyses more robust and transparent.

post-hoc decisions between different hypotheses. Moreover, we show that Bayes
factor estimates can be analyzed using modern statistical techniques such as
quantile-quantile plots and density plots. These tools can help to increase the
transparency of Bayes factor analyses, which is important for reproducibility

study the $SU(3)$ analogue of
anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model on the triangular lattice putting the
$p$-box symmetric representation on each site. Taking the large-$p$ limit, we
show that the low-energy effective theory is described by a $(2+1)$-dimensional
relativistic $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ nonlinear sigma model. Since the target space has a
nontrivial homotopy $\pi_2(SU(3)/U(1)^2)\simeq \mathbb{Z}^2$, this model has
two kinds of magnetic skyrmions, which can be created and annihilated by
monopole instantons. By careful analysis of the Wess-Zumino term in the spin
coherent path integral, we compute the Berry phase for these monopoles and it
produces the destructive interference. This restricts possible perturbations of
the effective Lagrangian by monopole operators, and we see that the
valence-bond-solid (VBS) phase should have degenerate ground states when
$p\not\in 3\mathbb{Z}$. We also compute 't Hooft anomalies to constrain
possible phases of this system, and a direct phase transition between N\'eel
and VBS phases is supported from the anomaly matching.
  The anomaly matching argument can also be applied to the $SU(4)$ analogue of
anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model on the triangular lattice. By
extending the field-theoretic study to the $SU(N)$ case, we can discuss how
the result for $N=3$ can be generalized to greater $N$. We may also add flavor
symmetry to these theories. In many cases, we can consistently combine 't
Hooft anomalies of spin and flavor symmetries. These theories on the triangular
lattice always have a N\'eel phase, but whether there is a VBS phase or not
depends on the representation on each site and whether $N$ is prime or not.
In the case of table-top quantum simulations, such as those using ultracold
atoms or ions, we can also study spin-coherent evolution with monopole
interactions. As mentioned above, whether such a system would really enter the
VBS phase or not depends on the number of spins $N_c$ that participate in the
simulation.

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there

overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors, as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty

methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently
even for function approximation, and there is even less work on solving partial
differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
on prototype problems, including problems with mixed input-output data, and
stochastic problems in high dimensions. In the Appendix, we include a
comprehensive description of all the UQ methods employed, which we will make
available as a Python package.

problems largely depends on the problem characteristics and data quality. While
state-of-the-art methods such as Deep Ensembles and MC dropout can produce
good results for medium-dimensional test functions and ReLU activated NNs, for
higher-dimensional test functions, more efficient methods that can reduce the
uncertainty estimation time significantly while maintaining accuracy are needed.

package that includes prototype problems in various dimensions, with and without
input-output data, as well as with and without stochastic components. The
package includes various UQ methods, and it has a user-friendly interface that
makes it easy to add or exchange methods as well as to implement custom
protocols for training and uncertainty quantification.

  Distributional semantics offers a promising approach to multilingual knowledge
and resource transfer by mapping words in different languages to a common
semantic space. Beyond word alignment, clustering has been explored as a way to
further project words that are not directly aligned to the common space. However
existing approaches either rely too heavily on expensive symmetric alignment
methods or use shallow character-level features. At the same time, thousands of
documented languages have linguistic structure knowledge bases that can be
incorporated into clustering. We introduce the Multi-MeAN dataset that extends
the classic English monolingual Multi-MeAN dataset to multiple languages. We
introduce the cluster-consistent correlational network that incorporates multiple
language knowledge bases for clustering and uses a deep correlational
architectural design to construct a consistent multilingual semantic space.
Intrinsic evaluation on monolingual and multilingual QVEC tasks shows that our
approach achieves significant gains over baselines. Extrinsically, we demonstrate
that our method is beneficial for automatic language annotation in the PROLD
task when using few annotations.

city, Santiago, suffered from widespread violence with public and private
infrastructure destruction. This work aims to expand an epidemiological
non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver results
resembling the observed spatial distribution of activity on Santiago. The main
reason for this failure can be attributed to the fact that the model lacks a
population displacement mechanism, which seems vital to explain Santiago's
unrest episodes.

coupled system of ordinary differential equations that incorporates non-local
terms. Due to the system's complexity, there is not an efficient analytical
method to study its behavior. In the case of the Chilean riots, the network's
topology did not seem to produce any significant dynamical pattern, as was the
case with the Paris riots model. However, defining an appropriate network
disconnection term to describe the withdrawal of subway service due to damage
could have been beneficial.
  In conclusion, although the proposed model has been able to explain the
temporal evolution of the French riots, it did not deliver the desired
results for Santiago's case. This failure might be due to the fact that the
model lacks a population displacement term, which seems crucial for Chile's
scenario.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., on overcast days
and water-filled ground, which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to
extract visual features. Experiments validate that it outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.
  We observe that recurrent models in existing learning based VIO tend to
accumulate error along time, which limits their performance behind state of the
arts. Therefore, we propose to utilize external memory attention to fuse visual
and inertial features for states estimation. This combines the advantage of
recurrent models in handling sequential data and the benefit of external memory
in modeling long-range dependency. With the help of external memory, recurrent
models can focus on recent features and avoid accumulating error, resulting in
much better performance. We validate that our proposed method outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.
  This paper proposes an end-to-end framework for visual-inertial odometry
(VIO) estimation, which exploits the information from camera and inertial sensors
to estimate position and translation. The framework exploits a deep learning
based framework to achieve VIO estimation. A modular long short-term memory (LSTM)
network is designed to simultaneously capture the visual and inertial
information. A data association module is further added to associate the
frames and estimate global position. To evaluate the proposed framework, a
high-fidelity simulation environment is built to simulate the real-world scenes
and several baselines are designed to compare the performance. The experimental
results indicate that the proposed framework can achieve better performance
compared to the classical baselines.

knowledge-amalgamation problem, termed
Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, to adapt the given teachers to the student, we developed
a novel strategy called Adversarial Filtered Proximal Policy Optimization
(AFP-PO), which incorporates two levels of control: proximal and adversarial.
The proximal control helps the decentralized teachers to agree on a common
space, where the student can be optimized based on the received features
instead of the high-dimensional weights. The adversarial control allows the
teachers to retain their own distinctive features, which are hostile to each
other, thus the student can be trained towards the target task that is
maximally distant from all of the teachers. Experiments show that the proposed
framework can achieve competitive results on both the main task and the
secondary tasks, validating its effectiveness for FedSA.

in the medial entorhinal cortex
of rat. Their peculiar firing patterns, which correlate with periodic locations
in the environment, led to early hypothesis that grid cells may provide some
form of metric for space. Subsequent research has since uncovered a wealth of
new insights into the characteristics of grid cells and related spatial
cell-types such as place cells and population codes. However, the question
whether grid cells encode a metric, and if so, of which kind, remains contentious
and open. Here we review recent findings on grid cells from geometry, physics
and engineering in order to provide a novel and formalized hypothesis on what
type of metric grid cells may encode: the Euclidean metric.
  From physics we know that the Euclidean metric is not the only one that is
fundamental, but it has unique properties that make it privileged in many
aspects of our life, e.g. architecture, engineering and communication. As we
will argue, the way grid cells encode distance in a metric invariant way
reminds strongly of the properties of the Euclidean metric. In addition,
recent findings on the scale invariance of grid cells can be seen as the
implementation of another important property of the Euclidean metric, namely
isotropy. We will discuss why this is different from other metric suggestions
such as the Manhattan metric and how recent experimental evidence supports our
thesis.
  In summary, our hypothesis is that the Euclidean metric is a functional
solution to the general problem of how to efficiently code for different
scales of the environment in a metric-invariant way. If so, this could have
important implications for our understanding of the rodent spatial
reprocessing system and may also be relevant for the transfer of inspiration
from nature to engineering.
  Finally, we would like to emphasize that our hypothesis is testable in a
brute-force way by simply looking at the correlation between grid cell fields
and Euclidean distance in different species. If grid cells code for
Euclidean distance then it should be possible to simply collapse the grid cell
fields by averaging over all directions at different scales.
  In conclusion, the present hypothesis showcases how insights from a wide
range of disciplines can be leveraged in order to tackle open questions in
neuroscience from a novel angle.

modulation of its composition by interior-exterior cycling. The formation and
evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and simulations. We emphasize the
importance of complementary studies between planetary formation and atmospheric
evolution for understanding the history of Venus. This work provides a
comprehensive view of the mechanisms which controlled the evolution of Venus's
atmosphere, and it may prove useful in developing more complex models for
investigating the history of Venus.
  This work provides a comprehensive view of the mechanisms which controlled the
evolution of Venus's atmosphere, and it may prove useful in developing more
complex models for investigating the history of Venus. While the framework
presented here could serve as a starting point for numerical models, these
models would need to incorporate coupled geochemical-geodynamic processes in a
consistent manner. Furthermore, verifying their outcomes with observational
constraints, when available, is crucial for confidently tracing the evolutionary
pathways of Venus.
  The exercise of tracing the evolution of Venus highlights the importance of
maintaining connections between formation and evolution processes. It shows that
these connections are crucial for preventing oversimplification of processes
occurring at different scales (from accretion to atmospheric interactions). It
also stresses that historical scenarios for Venus must not be constructed
post-hoc, but rather be built into models from the start. As more data are
obtained for Venus and other planets, developing consistent formation and

accuracy. We propose Selective Labeling to simplify the labeling task to
provide "yes/no" labels for candidate extractions predicted by a model trained
on partially labeled documents. We combine this with a custom active learning
strategy to find the predictions that the model is most uncertain about. We
show through experiments on document types drawn from 3 different domains that
selective labeling can reduce the cost of acquiring labeled data by $10\times$
with a negligible loss in accuracy.
  We also observe that the benefit of selective labeling depends on the domain,
and that domains that benefit the most are those that have long sequences that
contain many objects that can be predicted with modest uncertainty before more
labeling is done.
  We further observe that the choice of background image pixels to extract
text from using OCR can greatly affect model performance. Thus, we propose to
filter the pool of extractions by predicting the amount of background that
each one would contain. We train a complementary model on unlabeled documents to
make this prediction. We show that this can improve accuracy on a small labeled
set by $25\%$, thus greatly mitigating the cost savings provided by selective
labeling.
  Finally, we observe that many extractions that are clearly correct also get
labeled as such only after looking at the original image. We propose to predict
a "quality score" for each extraction, and select for human labeling only the
extractions with quality score 0. We get a $5\times$ savings in labeling cost
with a negligible loss in accuracy.

environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical and social interactions, raising questions on the social
impact of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income
diversity of interactions changes under different levels of spatial
segmentation in cities before and after the pandemic. Using de-identified
mobility data from more than 8 million mobile phone owners in 200 cities across
the US, China, India, Brazil, Russia, and Nigeria, we first reconstruct the
daily interaction networks at the neighborhood level and then analyze the
resulting network centrality distributions. We find that, before the pandemic,
highly segregated cities tend to have stronger spatial concentration of
interactions for low-income and high-income groups, while moderately segregated
cities tend to have more balanced interaction diversity. We also observe that
the pandemic leads to increased spatial concentration of interactions for both
low-income and high-income groups in all cities, and the underlying changes in
daily mobility patterns caused by the pandemic are more pronounced in highly
segregated and strongly centralized cities. Our analysis highlights the trade-offs
between the need for physical distancing and the need to preserve urban
diversity, and provides insights into the potential long-term social impacts of
pandemic-induced behavioral changes, stressing the importance of flexible
de-densification strategies that could adapt to local levels of segregation.

an overview about the combination of the
Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with two different approaches for Fluid-Structure
Interaction (FSI) problems, namely a monolithic and a partitioned approach. We
provide the details of implementation of two reduction procedures, and we then
apply them to the same test case of interest. We first implement a reduction
technique that is based on a monolithic procedure where we solve the fluid and
the solid problems all at once. We then present another reduction technique
that is based on a partitioned (or segregated) procedure: the fluid and the
solid problems are solved separately and then coupled using a fixed point
strategy. The toy problem that we consider is based on the Turek-Hron benchmark
test case, with a fluid Reynolds number Re = 100.
  We observe that both techniques are able to provide accurate results, but
with a considerable reduction in the dimension of the problem to be solved. As
the main contribution of this work is to provide an overview on how to perform
RBM for FSI problem, we make both the reduction procedures available in a
computational framework that can be easily downloaded and executed. This
framework is available in GitHub at https://github.com/Alfio-Bertino/RBM_for_FSI
and can be downloaded using Git (see details in Section I A) and run using
Matlab script (see details in Section I B).
  We believe that this work could be useful for anyone that is interested in
RBM for FSI problems, and in particular for those who are new in this field of
research. We make available two well-documented software programs that can be
easily compared and evaluated. This is particularly important for those
beginners in RBM for FSI who are just starting to explore this fascinating
field of research.
  We note that the software presented in this work is available for Matlab
script only. However, it is possible to transfer the algorithms presented in
this work to other programming languages such as C++ in collaboration with a
computational developer. The reader interested in this collaboration is
invited to contact the author at abertino@unige.ch.
  We also note that the FSI problem that we consider in this work is not
suitable for high Reynolds number because the reduced basis spaces that we
implement are not able to capture the turbulent structures that are
characterized by a mixing that is not aligned with the coordinate directions.

  HiTMap is a novel map representation for autonomous mobile robots to navigate
in unknown environments. Instead of using a global metric map, HiTMap adopts a
submap-based hierarchical topology which ensures the lightweight of drift-free
state estimation methods and only uses local metric maps for obstacle avoidance
to enhance navigation efficiency. Attached to the map as an attribute,
frontiers can be detected and used as navigation cues to drive the robots
preferentially approach the areas. Compared with traditional map representations
that directly use global metric maps, HiTMap can reduce the time to navigate and
enter the target area. Simulation experiments are conducted to evaluate the
performance of HiTMap, and the results show that it can reduce the time to enter
the target area by up to 45.8%. In addition, a set of real-world experiments are
performed using a differential wheeled mobile robot to validate the effectiveness
of HiTMap. The experiment results show that HiTMap can improve the navigation
efficiency by up to 35.1%.

a core theory for dependently typed
programming and higher-order constructive logic. Originally introduced in
Coquand's 1985 thesis, CC has inspired 25 years of research in programming
languages and type theory. Today, extensions of CC form the basis of languages
like Coq and Agda. This survey reviews three proofs of CC's strong
normalization property (the fact that there are no infinite reduction sequences
from well-typed expressions). It highlights the similarities in the approaches
while showing how their differences are motivated by the varying goals of their
authors.
  We introduce a general framework for the proof of strong normalization, and
we show that two previous proofs can be viewed as instantiations of this
framework. We also outline the main differences between our framework and the
third proof.
  Our framework demonstrates that CC's strict equality, by which every function
has exactly one representation, is responsible for the complexity of CC's
strong normalization proof. We discuss how the restriction of CC's equality to
strict functions is motivated by the role it plays in supporting modular
dependent programming, where a program's dependencies may involve complex
functions whose representations can be determined only by their arguments.
Finally, we show that a natural extension of CC with a strictness annotation
on function types can be proved strongly normalizing without the complexity
introduced by CC's strict equality.
  The framework presented here has been accepted for publication in a journal
article accompanying J. M. Smith's thesis work, which unified the first two
proofs into a single framework. That article provides a detailed comparison of
the three proofs, while this invitation-to-computer-science highlights the
main ideas from the proof framework and illustrates it through the example of
CC. Smith's framework demonstrates how CC's strong normalization proof can be
broken down into smaller, more manageable pieces, while this overview shows how
those pieces work together to produce the proof.

  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs that use only a
small, fixed, and often global set of object types and create objects in an
iterative manner during runtime. We call this pattern "incremental object
orientation." We propose a programming model that explicitly supports this
pattern and achieves both high memory locality and true SIMD parallelism on
accelerator devices via a simple data mapping strategy.
  To make incremental object orientation accessible to a wide range of
applications, we developed D3O, a first programming model that supports this
pattern directly. D3O compiles automatically generated C++ code that utilizes
popular object creation patterns into parallel programs for accelerator
devices, including GPUs and MICs. D3O further provides optional performance
enhancements in the form of performance-critical, low-level extensions.
  D3O achieves performance advantages of up to 4x, 2x, and 1.5x over the
state-of-the-art GPGPU librarieies CuBB and CUB on GPU devices, and up to 1.3x
and 2x over TBB and C++ Standard Library on MIC devices, for large-scale
applications from scientific computing, data compression and machine learning.
Our evaluation shows that it is possible to design programming models that
bring high performance to wide classes of object-oriented applications.
Further, our study reveals that even though many applications have an object
structure, very few parallel programs actually use object-oriented programming
in a meaningful way; most programs use objects only as a way to represent
low-level data structures.

known to be stable for long times. However, the physical conditions inside the
stellar interiors that allow these states are still a matter of research. It
has been formally demonstrated that both purely toroidal and purely poloidal
magnetic fields develop instabilities at some point in the star. On the other
hand, numerical simulations have proved the stability of roughly axisymmetric
magnetic field configurations inside stably stratified stars. These
configurations consist of mutually stabilizing toroidal and poloidal components
that work together to produce the net stability. For this reason, the
stability of magnetic fields in stars is still an open question. In this
manuscript we present a force-free configuration with coexisting toroidal and
poloidal magnetic fields that is exactly solved using a new approach based on
the Casimir method. This solution shows that the mutually stabilizing effect
between the toroidal and poloidal fields is, in fact, the same as the
stability of the exactly solved single-component field. Furthermore, it is
formally demonstrated that any small perturbation of the force-free
configuration preserves its exact solution, which indicates that the
configuration is not only stable but also rigorously stable. That is, once a
star forms with a magnetic field of this type, that field will persist for the
entire life of the star.
  Diving into the Dicke's casimir problem (1958), we have two charged
conducting sheets, with a capacitor being filled with the electromagnetic
vacuum. The solution shows that the fields in the vacuum region, which
mediates the interaction between the sheets, are, in fact, the exact
representations of a toroidal magnetic field and a poloidal magnetic field, as
seen in the Sun's atmosphere, for example. Furthermore, it is formally
demonstrated that the fields are rigorously stable, that is, any small
perturbation preserves the exact solution. The similarity between the void
regions of the casimir problem and the interior of a star is clear, which
leads to a new approach to exactly solve the problem of the stability of the
magnetic fields inside non-rigid stars.

trajectory of unoccupied RVs sequentially. To validate the effectiveness of the

learning scheme to improve the low-dose CT image quality without requiring

the cycleGAN approach is that it requires two deep neural network generators at
the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.
The secondary auxiliary generator is needed to enforce the cycle-consistency,
but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To address this issue, here we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting a routine-dose CT image to a low-dose CT image by simply changing
the AdaIN code by the opposite one. Here, the AdaIN code represents a
style/vector that controls the image style (e.g., sharpness, brightness) as
well as the intensity of the contrast enhancing structure. With this
proposed cycleGAN architecture, we successfully trained the model using only a
single low-dose CT image as a input without using any high-dose reference data
and evaluated its performance using a publicly available CT simulation package
called CT-Sim. The experimental results show that the proposed method could
restore a well-looked high-quality image similar to that trained with a pair
of low-dose/ high-dose CT images. We also observed that the proposed method
could effectively remove noise artifacts as well as enhance the diagnostic
image contrast without using any matching high-dose reference data.
Consequently, the proposed single cycleGAN architecture is shown to have great
potential in low-dose CT image enhancement without requiring any reference
image.

practical and effective in improving dialog understanding performance. However,
all existing contrastive learning methods for dialog understanding consider the
whole dialog as the unit of negative sampling, which may lose relevant

similar dialogs during pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPACE a tree
structured pre-trained conversation model which learns dialog representations
from labeled dialogs and unraveled dialog corpora via semi-supervised contrastive
pre-training. Concretely, we first define a general semantic tree structure (STS)
to unify the inconsistent annotation schema across different dialog datasets,
so that the rich structural information stored in all labeled data can be
exploited. Then we propose a tree structured score function to increase the
relevance of all possible dialogs that share similar tree structures and only
push away other completely different dialogs during supervised contrastive
pre-training. Experiments show that our method can achieve state-of-the-art
results on the DialogBART, DialoGLUE and Schema-Grounded Dialogue benchmarks

methods, we demonstrate that a model-based multi-task learner can benefit from

a model-free or a non-multi-task model-based learner. Besides that, the

  We introduce three popular model-based reinforcement learning algorithms to

scattering screens, most of

In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs. From the variability of the arc
orientation we have resolved six scattering screens along $\approx$4 pc of
interstellar line of sight towards the pulsar. Five of these screens are
oriented approximately perpendicular to the line of sight and are likely to be
the surfaces of molecular clouds. The sixth screen is oriented approximately
parallel to the line of sight and is more likely to be a sheet-like structure,
such as the edge of a cloud or a galactic density wedge. We present a model of
the scattering screens and discuss the relation between the resolved screens
and observed interstellar extinction and H{\small I} columns towards the pulsar.
The extension of this analysis to a larger sample of pulsars will provide a
statistically meaningful investigation of the relation between scattering and
extinction in the interstellar medium.

performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The

state-of-the-art architecture for pixel-level segmentation, training it on a
public dataset of WSIs and a large private dataset, to benchmark our pixel
annotation technique. We also train a classification model to evaluate our
polyps classification annotation. Our models achieve outstanding results both on
the tested WSIs and on the standalone instances. This evidence confirms the
quality of our dataset and highlights the superiority of deep learning over
hand-crafted features for medical image analysis. This work is an important

a suitable incoming plane wavelet with compact support in the propagation
direction; \emph{ii)} solving a scattering problem in the time domain for the
incoming plane wavelet; \emph{iii)} reconstruction of the time-harmonic
solution from the time-domain solution via a Fourier transform in time. An
essential ingredient of the new method is a front-tracking mesh adaptation
algorithm for solving the problem in \emph{ii)}. By exploiting the limited
support of the wave front, this allows us to make the number of the required
degrees of freedom to reach a given accuracy significantly less dependent on
the frequency $\omega$. We also present a new algorithm for computing the
Fourier transform in \emph{iii)} that exploits the reduced number of degrees of
freedom corresponding to the adapted meshes. Numerical examples demonstrate the
advantages of the proposed method and the fact that the method can also be
applied with external source terms such as point sources and sound-soft
scatterers. The gained efficiency, however, is limited in the last two cases.

2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction cases is reduced to be the same as the fa
cilities' self-interaction. The proposed algorithm is particularly useful when
the number of facilities is large and their supports are all contained within
the same domain. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed
method by solving a system of volume integral equations, which is equivalent to
and yet more general than the classical single-domain near field problem. The
results show that the proposed method can provide second-order errors in the
same number of operations as the direct quadrature method for smaller facilities
but with a significant reduction in the number of iterations required to
converge. For larger facilities, the proposed method provides fourth-order
errors.

structure of the matrix to be applied. In this paper, we present an algorithm
